Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.
  • The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
  • It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

It has been revealed that with The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh notes, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the problems that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

In a recent development, “I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”.

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Sources indicate that next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

It has been revealed that phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she indicates has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that the Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#22434. Latest Update: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

Latest Update: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • In a recent development, if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

In a recent development, if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

“The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sources indicate that sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, claims Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that the textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin indicates. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin indicates.

Industry observers note that because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

It has been revealed that women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, indicates Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

Recent findings suggest that and it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin states. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

In a recent development, home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin claims. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

Industry observers note that that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health complications.

In a recent development, if left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, says Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really promptly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

According to recent reports, over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra says, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition problems and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar says. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research shows that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s crucial to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

#22433. Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.
  • In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.
  • The 20×20 series, released to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a massive impact on the next 20.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20×20 series, released to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a massive impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a upcoming wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier’s Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.

For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

“Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” noted Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful.”.

Sources indicate that the Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.

According to recent reports, their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous. They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play.

Quickly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” said Abascal.

“And also how to plan for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”.

The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza. Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since].

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all people.

“It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” said Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a organization after that.”.

The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.

“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she remarked.

“Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”.

As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.

It has been revealed that arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

“We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo said. “We analyse what’s the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”.

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.

“The main concern is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” stated Abascal.

The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract.

That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.

“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.

When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.

“I’m the bad cop,” he says with a smile.

But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

“I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” remarked Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it’s things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”.

“And it’s not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”.

For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.

“I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” stated Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”.

It has been revealed that lanza Atelier’s slate currently includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on bird migration and pregnancy. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year plan – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.

The country has been in the spotlight in the last few years as one of the few in Latin America with a progressive government, and one whose president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has frequently had to stand her ground against its northern neighbour.

Asked about whether government policy has had any positive effect on architecture and related industries at home, Abascal and Arienzo’s good cop and bad cop come out.

“From architects of the older generation, our generation and the younger generation, I can feel a sense of optimism,” said Abascal.

In a recent development, “I feel a sense of doing nothing,” said Arienzo. “Claudia is way better than what there was before; I’m a leftie. But I think there should be many more competitions around housing in the city.”.

Both say they would like to see more public competitions in place of private developments, and that they would eagerly enter.

According to recent reports, “Mexico City’s downtown is beautiful and it’s almost empty,” said Arienzo. “There isn’t a lot of density. I think it should be much more about that. Housing is a big problem and will be forever for these big cities.”.

There is an ideal future for the architects, then. It’s one that would see the urban landscape of their home city benefit from the respect, creativity and serene beauty that is the Lanza calling card.

Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

#22430. Industry News: Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (913 w)

Industry News: Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended).
  • But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about new plasma as an anti-aging elixir.
  • Industry observers note that plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about new plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Industry observers note that plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

Sources indicate that “It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she states.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he claims. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”.

According to recent reports, about 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

In a recent development, “So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” states Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

Sources indicate that at first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

According to recent reports, “If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she indicates.

Part of the reason for this, notes Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, says Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be vital to find out for whom this works.”.

Sources indicate that as a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” indicates Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”.

CAN combines eclectic references for eccentric revamp of London house

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.
  • Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a new kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Jim Stephenson.

Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House-Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.

Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.

Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a new kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.

Meanwhile, the design was required to be an expression of the interests and experiences of its clients – designer Fabiane Lee-Perrella, television producer Robin Lee-Perrella and their two sons.

“The atmospheric side of the brief was to somehow encapsulate the clients’ diverse visual tastes and architectural memories from their pasts,” CAN founder Mat Barnes told Dezeen.

“This resulted in the eclecticism of the project; one that is very personal to the clients.”.

Visual references given to CAN included modernist Brazilian architecture projects such as Lina Bo Bardi’s SESC Pompéia in São Paulo, as well as industrial architecture, David Hockney paintings and Moroccan riads.

The resultant design inspired the project’s name, House Tropicália, which nods to the late 1960s Tropicália movement that celebrated bold ideas and rebelled against accepted norms.

“We reject the idea that a project needs to be driven by a single, homogeneous idea or material,” noted Barnes.

“Instead, we celebrate the complexity, diversity and even contradiction inherent in our clients’ tastes and design references,” he continued.

“We see these different influences not as competing ideas, but as an opportunity to create something individual and ultimately more meaningful.”.

The focal point of the project is its highly unique rear elevation, with features including two towers of engineering drainage tubes, which break through a red-steel canopy that extends over the patio.

Meanwhile, bright blue and red fibre-cement panels decorate its elevation, alongside portions of textured raked render and exposed concrete, punctured by irregular shapes.

Details also include a metal sawtooth roof at first-floor level, alongside a bright yellow screen facing the neighbouring property to prevent overlooking.

Finally, at ground level, a full-width set of doors open onto a patio with a winding perimeter, referencing the designs of Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx.

It has been revealed that “It brings together a mix of materials, forms and ideas drawn from the huge range of references the clients shared with us,” mentioned Barnes. “I think it captures the character and personalities of the clients brilliantly.”.

It has been revealed that inside, the back half of the ground floor has been rearranged to maximise its connection to the rear garden. This is where the new open-strategy kitchen, dining and living space is positioned.

Meanwhile, at the front of the ground floor, the studio has created a secondary dining area and living space, and a children’s playroom in the original lounge.

Above, a void on the north side of the first floor has been filled to add a main bedroom suite, complete with an ensuite and roof terrace. Another bedroom has also been added.

The roof terrace has a walk-on, diamond-shaped skylight, which sits directly above the dining table.

Sources indicate that interior finishes echo the eclecticism of the exterior, with a bold mix of colours, materials and textures. This includes exposed steel joists and trusses, and a colourful timber kitchen with contrasting black tiles.

Walls of ceramic tiles on the ground floor have shell-like forms, handmade by Fabiane Lee-Perrella with glazing that shifts from pink to blue hues.

A microcement floor runs throughout the ground floor and incorporates pebble inlay that evokes a river and is a nod to the water feature at SESC Pompéia.

CAN hopes the project will highlight the importance of challenging the “established or standard way of doing things in a particular city or context”.

“We think it’s vital to look beyond the usual architectural references and draw inspiration from unexpected places, whether that be sculpture, set design, or even infrastructure,” Barnes said.

Industry observers note that “These disciplines can offer entirely different ways of thinking about space, material and form. Ultimately, it’s about exposing clients to these different ways of doing things.”.

CAN, known fully as Critical Architecture Network, was founded by Barnes in 2016. Its previous projects include the equally bold house extensions Druid Grove and Mountain View.

Photography by Jim Stephenson.

#22427. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1068 w)

Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people.
  • In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

Recent findings suggest that if you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller notes, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

It has been revealed that at the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.).

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

In a recent development, both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller claims. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.).

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

According to recent reports, whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran states. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she claims.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller says. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

Industry observers note that if you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.

Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.

Atelier Manferdini founder Elena Manferdini, who is Italian and teaches at Sci-Arc in Los Angeles, noted that her studio sought to translate the largely functional structure into something more human.

“Critical infrastructure is essential to our cities, yet the Dominion Energy substation is fundamentally designed for machines rather than people,” Manferdini told Dezeen.

“With inVisible, we wanted to explore this dichotomy, transforming a purely functional structure into something meaningful to the surrounding community,” she continued.

“While the interior responds to the needs of machines, the exterior becomes an opportunity to engage with people through color, pattern, and perception, creating a dialogue between infrastructure and the human scale of the city.”.

The substation converts power into different voltages to facilitate the transmission of energy, and the patterns on the sculptural facade were computationally designed to represent that process.

Atelier Manferdini used programming site Processing, which came out of the MIT Media Lab in the early 2000s, to design the colourful tile band that lines the bottom of the structure.

This pattern incorporates 10 colours and tiles of three different sizes, two, four, and six inches across – a reference to voltages – along with “glitches” in the program to create the graphic.

It recalls the Boogie Woogie works of modernist artist Piet Mondrian, which were based on the rhythms of cities.

Above the ceramic pattern, the studio placed massive gridded aluminium panels.

The panels create a ventilated facade system, set at different distances from the exterior walls and stacked where they meet so that sunlight passes through different densities in the gridded pattern, creating a variable light effect.

“The folds catch light and cast shadows, allowing the surface to shift with the time of day and the viewer’s position,” said the studio.

At night, the panels are backlit by programmable LEDs.

Overall, the studio remarked that it considers the contrast between the monochromatic metal and colour tile patterns a unified image.

“Quiet and metallic above, saturated and granular below, the two bands form a unified architectural composition,” noted the studio, with the unseen machines humming with electricity inside.

Other creative takes on infrastructure include a power station in China that Schmidt Hammer Lassen shrouded with steel lamellas and topped with a walkway, as well as a sculptural stormwater facility in Toronto by GH3, a Canadian studio well known for its aesthetic treatment of otherwise overlooked infrastructure.

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated.

Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism.
  • Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight.
  • It has been revealed that metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

The truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

It has been revealed that metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

In short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, says Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

Recent findings suggest that that mentioned, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research shows that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Recent findings suggest that every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

Recent findings suggest that this can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

Strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

Industry observers note that by strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison says what’s most key is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

Industry observers note that protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

In a recent development, however, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, states doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

Recent findings suggest that for most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That remarked, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

According to recent reports, an often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of concerns, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research highlights that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research shows chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

There is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

#22419. 7 Tips for Building a Healthy Diet With Canned, Frozen, and Packaged Goods

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1498 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

7 Tips for Building a Healthy Diet With Canned, Frozen, and Packaged Goods

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch.
  • Industry observers note that but this suggestion is hardly fair.
  • According to recent reports, besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch. Oftentimes, their videos carry an implicit sense of moral superiority, suggesting that you’re not a good parent (or at least not as good as them) if you’re resorting to pre-packaged store-bought items. Those who pick their own produce and painstakingly hand-craft their own candy necklaces simply work harder, love their children more, are fundamentally better.

Industry observers note that but this suggestion is hardly fair. For the vast majority of people—meaning those who don’t make their living off of wellness content or have near-endless amounts of time and money to burn—canned, frozen, and packaged stuff is almost always a far more practical option. “Groceries are a fortune,” after all, Anthea Levi, MS, RD, a Brooklyn-based health writer and the founder of Alive+Well Nutrition, tells SELF—and fresh items tend to be the most expensive, as a trip to the produce section of the supermarket will readily prove.

According to recent reports, besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power. “You can keep them in your freezer for months, so that often gives people confidence” in the purchase, since they know they don’t have an expiration date hanging over their head, Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. This, in turn, leads to reduced food waste: “Fresh salad greens are notorious for going slimy in the fridge, but you’ll never have that glitch with frozen spinach. Ditto for fish. Fresh fish needs to be cooked ASAP before it turns, while frozen fish and canned or tinned fish last until you’re ready to use them,” Levi indicates.

Nielsen also takes matter with the basic idea that these options are somehow inherently inferior—“a major, big misconception,” in her eyes. “There has been a lot of confusion about the nature of these foods in general. Just because something is processed or packaged does not mean it’s unhealthy,” she states.

According to recent reports, in other words, canned, frozen, or packaged items are often perfectly fine to include in your diet—and you shouldn’t feel embarrassed, ashamed, or inadequate if they make frequent appearances in your meals (or if they’re your first resort over fresh). “Constant access to fresh foods is, unfortunately, a luxury. If canned, frozen, or packaged items are the only way you’re able to put a fruit or vegetable on your plate, go for it,” Levi notes. But if you’re still concerned about the health aspect, there are a few key ways to maximize the nutritional value and improve the overall experience. Here’s what to know to make the most of your freezer stash.

Sources indicate that “Typically, the fewer ingredients, the better,” Levi indicates—a rule of thumb to consider while shopping. While canned, frozen, and packaged items have a reputation for being ultra-processed—rife with additives and lower in nutritional value—there are actually plenty out there “that are made from just one or two whole-food ingredients, such as canned peas, frozen fruit, and canned salmon,” Levi says. “These are as close to fresh foods as you can get, and just as nutritious.” Many jarred peanut butters only contain dry roasted peanuts and salt, for example. (By contrast, Ritz peanut butter crackers, which have an ingredients list several rows long, are a very different story.).

In a recent development, that said, this issue can be nuanced. “Just because an ingredient looks fancy or technical or like a chemical does not necessarily mean that it's bad for you,” Nielsen points out. Many processed foods—including bread, milk, and breakfast cereal—are fortified with healthy vitamins and minerals that you might not otherwise consume enough of in your diet. Take vitamin C—which may appear under the name “ascorbic acid”—as an example. “You might not recognize that what you’re looking at is vitamin C, so you don't want to scare yourself off of potentially nutritious and valuable food because you see things on the ingredients label that you don't recognize,” Nielsen indicates.

In Nielsen’s experience, canned foods are often considered even less “healthy” than frozen, but the stigma isn’t necessarily warranted. Canned beans, which boast fiber, plant-based protein, and minerals like iron and zinc, are an excellent example of a canned food that amounts to an “incredible nutrition source,” she claims. Still, this category does have one major drawback: Staples like veggies, soups, and, yes, beans can contain a significant amount of sodium, a mineral that can cause high blood pressure and related issues like heart disease and stroke when overconsumed. Tinned fish like TikTok’s beloved sardines can suffer from the same issue, as the brine inside the tin can be heavy on added salt as well.

Sources indicate that given that many brands offer sodium-sensitive alternatives, try to prioritize those options instead to keep your sodium intake in check and avoid potential health consequences, according to Nielsen. Look for labels like “No salt added,” “Low sodium,” or even “No sodium” to steer you in the right direction. If you can’t find anything fitting that bill at your local store, draining and rinsing canned products before use can also drastically cut down on the sodium content—by up to 40%, according to some estimates. (Just keep in mind this method may also cause losses in other nutrients, like vitamin C.).

Sources indicate that “In terms of packaged and processed foods, I'm always looking for a couple of nutrients to minimize and a couple of nutrients to optimize,” Nielsen notes. Sodium is one to limit or avoid, as we’ve already covered, but there are others too—like added sugars and saturated fat. “Peaches that come canned in sugary syrup aren’t as nutritious as peaches that come canned in water, or are purchased frozen or fresh,” for example, Levi says.

Sources indicate that on the other hand, when you’re reading over a nutrition facts label, “what you want to see is fiber,” Nielsen indicates—and “protein is a big bonus.” Multiple vitamins and minerals in a product is also often a positive sign. Even breakfast cereals, which are often thought of as unhealthy, “can be incredible sources of minerals like iron and zinc—things that we need that help to keep our metabolism running, that keep us energized,” Nielsen says.

Trying to decide between two (or more) similar products? Comparing and contrasting the ingredients can help you narrow it down, according to Nielsen. Take breakfast cereal: You’ll want to ask yourself, “‘Which one of these cereals gives me the most fiber, the most protein, has the least sugar?’” she notes. In this case, the relative content of vitamins and minerals can also be a helpful clue. Seeing that a cereal contains 10% to 20% of your recommended dietary allowance, as many do, can be “your sort of gut check that this is actually a really nutritious food,” Nielsen says.

Even though frozen veggies are affordable and durable, they do have one big downside compared to fresh: Their taste and texture can take a hit—and, in turn, “you do have to adjust your cooking somewhat,” Nielsen says. To prevent sogginess, cook frozen veggies from frozen rather than letting them defrost first, according to Levi. And you’ll want to use heat-based cooking methods (like air-frying, baking, roasting, and stir-frying) “as opposed to water-based methods like boiling or steaming,” she says.

According to recent reports, “Many of us are working more than ever before—maybe working two or three jobs—and we don't have a lot of time to put a home-cooked meal on the table,” Nielsen says. Strategically pairing your canned, frozen, and packaged items is an easy way to boost efficiency in the kitchen without sacrificing nutritional value. If you’re having canned soup for dinner, you can dump in a can of lentils to boost the fiber and protein, for example. (Bonus tip: You can also use this approach to stretch out your leftovers. Need a batch of spaghetti to last longer? Toss some frozen peas on top or some frozen broccoli on the side.).

Recent findings suggest that “Stocking your freezer and pantry with budget-friendly canned, frozen, and packaged items can help make balanced meals a breeze,” Levi claims. Follow the tried-and-true “plate method” to guarantee a nutritious result, according to Nielsen: Reserve a quarter of your plate for whole grains or starchy vegetables, another quarter for protein, and the remaining half for fruits and non-starchy veggies. You could make rolled oats with chia seeds, frozen berries, and peanut butter for breakfast, or pasta with tinned sardines and frozen broccoli for dinner, for example, Levi says. “It sounds way too simple, but it is backed by so much science to help you balance your diet without counting anything,” Nielsen says. “As long as you stick to that plate method, you will be eating a nourishing diet”—yes, even if your ingredients don’t come to you direct.
