13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

📅 18 Oct 2021 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story.
  • It has been revealed that but here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight.
  • The stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story. Black women are diagnosed with breast cancer at a younger median age (60, compared with 62 for white women) and are 38% more likely to die from the disease. They have the lowest survival rate for every known stage of breast cancer. And about one in five Black women with breast cancer are diagnosed with hard-to-treat triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), more than any other racial or ethnic group.

It has been revealed that but here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight. Black women have always been more than a data point, and perhaps nowhere is that truer than in the way they face, survive, and remake their lives after a breast cancer diagnosis.

The stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic. They are individuals with careers, children, humor, faith, rage, and joy whose experiences with breast cancer changed them in ways both devastating and profound. In finding their own paths through treatment and beyond, they’ve built something the data can’t quantify: community, purpose, and a hard-won blueprint for survival they’re passing on to every woman who comes after them.

In a recent development, monique Bass, 53, had always been proactive about her health. A single mother of twin sons and grandmother of four, she started getting annual mammograms at 40. But it was a self-exam at 47 while lying in bed one night that changed everything. She found a lump that didn’t feel right.

Recent findings suggest that what followed were three tissue biopsies of the lump over three years, each coming back benign. Doctors wanted to keep monitoring. Bass pushed back. The lump was growing, and she knew her body well enough to realize something was wrong. She insisted they remove the lump (a procedure called a lumpectomy) and test it. The diagnosis: stage 1 invasive ductal carcinoma that was aggressive enough to require immediate chemotherapy.

Bass got the call while sitting in a car wash. “I felt like I was in The Twilight Zone,” she notes. “Not in a million years did I think I would ever hear the words, ‘You have cancer.’” The timing made everything harder. It was 2020, the height of the pandemic, so she navigated much of her journey alone. Adding “another emotional layer,” she was also going through a divorce. Treatment included four rounds of doxorubicin, four rounds of paclitaxel, and 21 radiation treatments. Losing her hair hit the hardest. “But the silver lining is that it grew back even more beautifully after treatment,” Bass says.

Throughout it all her faith anchored her. “I’m not a deeply religious person, but I believe in God, and I knew he had me in the palm of his hand,” Bass indicates. On the other side of treatment, she founded What’s Behind the Bra?, a Upcoming Jersey nonprofit that distributes comfort care packages to breast cancer patients year-round and hosts a weekly podcast of the same name every Sunday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

Jaqueline Beale, 64, comes from a family with a long history of cancer, including her mother, who had breast cancer. That’s why it wasn’t a huge surprise when, at 40, she found a lump during a breast self-exam. Even though a sonogram and mammogram came back clear, it was obvious that something wasn’t right, so Beale got a biopsy.

When the radiologist called with her result—stage 1 breast cancer, which means the cancer hadn’t spread beyond where the abnormal cells had developed—she could hear a lot of noise in the background. He said, “I’m in New York trying to hail a cab, but you have breast cancer. You need to find a breast surgeon.” Despite the bluntness, Beale notes she couldn’t help but find the humor in the situation, which is something she carried with her through treatment.

“I made sure that I surrounded myself with laughter and love,” she says, “and I told my family that I knew they loved me, but I also needed a lot of laughter to get through it.”.

In a recent development, she recalls one incident in an elevator after her sister had taken her to a chemo treatment. “I had been sick as a dog after, and a woman got in and asked if I was okay. My sister remarked, ‘Oh, she’s fine. She’s just got a little bit of cancer.’ The woman looked horrified, but I laughed. My family knew that their sense of humor is what I needed.”.

It has been revealed that annita White, 51, was five months late for her mammogram. As a single mother of two boys, a higher education administrator, and a first-year PhD student, she always had something more pressing. When she finally went, she expected the usual letter in the mail saying everything was fine. Instead, she got a call. There was a mass that hadn’t been there before.

Recent findings suggest that by the time the biopsy came back, she already knew. A technician had commented on how hard the mass was, and White felt the diagnosis in her spirit before the words were ever spoken. The confirmation came the next day. “When I got the call, I fell to the floor and cried tears of desperation,” she states. “My first thought was, ‘Lord, I can’t do this.’”.

What followed was hard in every way: chemotherapy, losing her breasts, losing her hair, which had always been full. “Being bald left me feeling vulnerable and insecure,” White says. “Physically, losing my breasts and going through chemotherapy made me feel like my body was no longer my own.” Through it all the fear that drove her was running out of time—time to see her sons become men and to meet her grandchildren someday.

Recent findings suggest that her faith, which she’d been privately wrestling with for years, met her exactly where she was. She’d been asking God to truly show up in her life. “He did,” she says. “In the middle of one of the hardest seasons of my life, he carried me through.”.

Three years later White is cancer-free, her hair is back, and she recently finished her PhD. She now walks in her purpose as Dr. Nita, a member of the African American Breast Cancer Alliance survivor network, sharing her story and those of others facing the disease. “What once felt like the end became the beginning of something greater,” she notes.

In a recent development, marylande Regis, 38, had been in her newly introduced Georgia home for four months when everything changed. A registered nurse, realtor, wife, and mother of three, she had just stopped breastfeeding her nine-month-old when she found the lump. Her baby had never latched well on that side. When she messaged her provider, the on-call response was that it was probably a clogged milk duct and that she was too young to worry about it being something more serious. Regis didn’t accept that. She called back and left a message, insisting that something was wrong. “Another ob-gyn saw the message and encouraged me to make an office appointment immediately,” she states. Within two weeks she had a diagnosis: aggressive stage 2B, BRCA1-positive breast cancer. Within two more weeks what had been one tumor and one impacted lymph node had become three tumors and four impacted lymph nodes. Regis was 36.

In a recent development, “I was relieved that I advocated for myself,” she says. “I was proud that fear didn’t factor into my decision.”.

It has been revealed that what followed was relentless. Regis went through six months of chemotherapy, a bilateral mastectomy, six weeks of radiation, a total hysterectomy (to eliminate her body’s main source of estrogen), and breast reconstruction, all over a span of roughly 18 months. She lost friends to cancer along the way, as well as a cousin diagnosed around the same time. Her faith was, as Regis describes it, “shaken and stirred and flipped every way possible.” She wrote the notable letters. She wrote her own obituary. She was practical about it. “I wanted to be positive, but I am also very realistic,” Regis says.

Recent findings suggest that the hardest part wasn’t any single treatment—it was losing control. As her family’s go-to planner for everything from doctor’s appointments to vacations, she found it foreign to ask for help. But when she told her parents, her mother demonstrated up and never left. “We joke, but my mom never went home,” Regis says. “This is her house now.” Her husband, Kory, came to every appointment and held steady even through both of them losing their jobs. “He deserves a trophy,” she says.

In a recent development, as the daughter of Haitian immigrants, raised to be everything her parents couldn’t be, Regis claims the fight was never just medical. Today strength looks different than it did before cancer. It looks like making it to the bus stop with her son, who has autism. It looks like seeing her oldest finish nursing school and work toward becoming an ob-gyn. It looks like watching her youngest hit milestones like learning to talk. “I would have missed that if I didn’t fight,” she says. “The clouds are moving. The sun has decided to show itself. I can’t wait to soak it all in.”.

Illness had always been an afterthought for 75-year-old Judy Fambrough-Billingsley. Why would it cross her mind? She walked three miles every day, swam laps all summer, took Zumba classes, and played soccer for 30 years. Judy Fambrough-Billingsley had never smoked or drank, and she didn’t even need to take medication. Being healthy wasn’t something she worked at; it was just who she was. A naturalized American citizen born in Germany, she traveled back to her home country regularly to visit family. Her life was full and active.

Recent findings suggest that so when she felt a lump—and then another six months later—she ignored them. After all, she’d had a clean mammogram earlier that year. But when she noticed them growing and multiplying, she went back to her doctor. The results were not what she expected.

In a recent development, “I was shocked,” Fambrough-Billingsley notes. She suddenly found herself navigating an entirely new set of experiences: prescription bottles, hospital procedures, lab processes—the whole medical system. “Being a part of a world where sickness exists had never been my world until now,” she says.

Industry observers note that what carried her through was far older than her diagnosis. She grew up during the Civil Rights Era, the daughter of a successful Black entrepreneur who built his business during tumultuous years in US history. Both her parents were lifetime members of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). She was president of the NAACP Youth Council and an active member of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Fambrough-Billingsley knows something about fighting for your life in systems that weren’t built for you.

Recent findings suggest that “Growing up during the Civil Rights Era contributed to this era of fighting,” she says. “Never giving up.” That same spirit—the one her parents modeled, the one she fell into during her work as a community organizer and across decades of a life fully lived—is the one she’s bringing to this too. She may still be on her breast cancer journey, but this is not her first fight.

Taylor Johnson was nearly 30 when she found the lump on her left breast. A mom and content creator who loves trying fresh things and staying active, she went to her primary care doctor, who referred her for an ultrasound and a mammogram. Johnson was denied a mammogram—she was told she was too young. She pushed anyway, got a biopsy (in lieu of the mammogram), and days later, had a diagnosis: stage 2 triple-negative breast cancer.

Industry observers note that “My reaction was a very deep pause, trying to process what my doctor had told me,” Johnson says. “It then hit me, and all I could do was cry.”.

She’s in the middle of her treatment initiative, which includes six months of chemotherapy, followed by surgery and three weeks of radiation. After finishing chemo Johnson felt confident that would be the hardest part of her journey, both physically and emotionally. But her own health wasn’t her only concern: She knew her five-year-old was watching her every move, and she wanted to stay stable for her daughter. “I was so used to always being the strong one,” Johnson indicates. “This definitely tested that.” She held it together not because it came easily, but because she understood what her daughter was absorbing.

Sources indicate that she is grateful for the community that rallied around her while she waited. Weekly prayer calls, rotating visits from family and friends, and a medical team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona that went above and beyond carried her through.

Though Johnson hasn’t finished treatment yet, completing chemo clarified something for her. “It has reassured me how strong I truly am,” she notes. Strength, she’s learned, isn’t just physical. The emotional and mental muscle it takes to keep going counts just as much.

Jessica Ncube, 41, built her life around caring for others. A licensed clinical social worker, the co-owner of a mental health practice, and a mom, she was always in motion. Her life revolved around showing up for others and helping them navigate their hardest moments. “Looking back I do not know that I was always receiving,” she says.

Industry observers note that her diagnosis came quietly. A routine mammogram caught it; nothing in her body had felt amiss. That silence, Ncube says, is exactly why early detection matters. When she got the news she went into survival mode. “You hear the words, but it takes time for them to land,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that ncube’s journey started with a lumpectomy. When her margins came back unclear, meaning the pathologist could not determine whether all the cancerous cells were removed, she made the decision to move forward with a double mastectomy with reconstructive surgery. “Losing a part of your body, even when it is lifesaving, is still a loss,” she says. “The hardest part was learning how to sit in both gratitude and grief at the same time.”.

As someone professionally wired to be strong for others, letting that tendency go was its own kind of work. “Strength became less about holding everything in and more about being honest about what I needed,” Ncube claims. Her faith grounded her, and her community revealed up, but she also had to unlearn something deeply familiar. “As a Black woman there is a resilience that is almost ingrained in us,” she says. “I had to learn how to balance that resilience with softness.”.

It has been revealed that after completing treatment Ncube has become more present and deliberate. Her definition of strength has changed entirely. “Strength today is softness. It is honesty. It is allowing myself to receive, to rest, and to not have all the answers,” she states.

In a recent development, ameiko Newman, 40, didn’t learn of her diagnosis through a routine screening. She was rushed to the hospital for abdominal pain, and that’s when she learned she had breast cancer. Life before her diagnosis had been stressful, uncertain, a season of not quite knowing where she was headed. In a strange way, cancer gave her direction.

“For me, cancer saved me,” she says. “It made me a better person. It made me fight harder, push through the hard times and know what I want in life.”.

Newman is still in treatment, receiving chemotherapy and immunotherapy every week, and she is honest about what that looks like: There are good days and bad days. She goes to church faithfully, prays every day, and tries to stay positive through it all.

What has surprised her most is that in the middle of fighting for her own life, she found her purpose: helping others fight for theirs. Newman rebranded her business entirely around that mission and started designing scarves with chemo patients in mind. “I started making them mainly for my Black women because you know we love having style,” she says. But a wide variety of women from all over have since bought them.

She wakes up every day, gets her kids ready, works out, and moves through life. Faith, she states, is what makes that possible. Her message to any Black woman who’s just gotten diagnosed is both simple and hard-won: “Cancer doesn’t define you. You define you. Even though you’re fighting for your life, help someone else fight for theirs.”.

Charlotte Connor, 38, had just undergone a breast augmentation when she felt a lump in her breast. “When I saw my doctor, they weren’t concerned, in part because of my young age,” says Connor, who was 30 years old at the time. She had a mammogram and ultrasound to check for signs of cancer, but no MRI. “Looking back now I wish I would have asked for that MRI,” she says.

In a recent development, at the first checkup six months later, they told her she was fine. At the second—one year after the original lump was found—the lump had tripled in size. Her doctor ordered a biopsy, and her diagnosis was confirmed: stage 2A ductal carcinoma, which means the cancer was growing but contained to the breast and surrounding lymph nodes.

Sources indicate that “When they told me I had cancer, I was calm,” she says. Her mindset immediately shifted from a sinking feeling to being optimistic about the future. “I focused on getting healthy again,” says Connor, who started fantasizing about what she would do after treatment.

She remembers thinking, I may be feeling sick and throwing up from chemotherapy, but what restaurants am I going to go to after all this is over? It’s an outlook that didn’t necessarily come naturally to her, either. “I’m not even overly optimistic in life—I think I’m a realist—but in this situation, I shifted to being overly optimistic.”.

According to recent reports, part of that mindset shift was for her young daughter. “I couldn’t be pessimistic; I had to be strong for her,” she indicates. “And I knew that how I acted in this situation was how she was going to mirror things and react to stressful situations when she got older.”.

Connor’s other pillar of support came from a tight-knit circle of friends and family, who threw her a head-shaving party before she lost her hair due to chemo. “Making things fun and lighthearted like that got me through my darkest, saddest moments,” she states.

It was 1999, and Donna Culmer had just received a clean mammogram. A few months later she felt a stone-size bump on her right side, so she went back to her ob-gyn to get it checked out. They redid the mammogram on both breasts, and while what she’d felt was actually a fibrocystic lump, the imaging found a small, not palpable spot on her left side that turned out to be a stage 1 cancer. “I was stunned,” Culmer notes. “I didn’t even know what questions to ask.” She drove back to work in a daze and told her boss what had happened.

Sources indicate that at 46 she was serving in the Navy as an instructor and trainer to personnel who were working alongside the Marines. She was married to a Marine and raising three children. There was no good moment for this. There never is.

According to recent reports, four months of chemotherapy followed, with nausea and exhaustion that never quite let up. Her doctors were concerned that the chemo might not work, so she had a mastectomy. Through it all her community refused to let her go through it alone. Her father drove her to every session and sat with her. Her church came to her, literally; services were held at her house.

Twenty-seven years later, Culmer, now 73, has had time to reflect. “As Black women, we have been through challenges our whole lives,” she says. “This is just one more.” Her advice is practical and clear. “Don’t panic and ask questions, even if you have to write them down,” Culmer says. “The treatments available now are so much better than what I had.”.

In a recent development, one morning, Patricia Fox, 38, woke up with a lump in her right breast that wasn’t there the night before—she was just 26 years old at the time. Fox scheduled an appointment with her ob-gyn that day. “They told me that I was a young Black woman and had dense breasts, and it was likely a cyst,” she notes. “They were ready to turn me away.”.

The lump, which was a little smaller than a golf ball, seemed strange to Fox. Thankfully, she listened to her intuition. “There was something telling me to get it checked out,” she indicates, so her doctor did a biopsy just to be sure.

In a recent development, her results came back as estrogen receptor-positive stage 2A breast cancer, meaning her cancer had estrogen receptors that would respond to hormone therapy drugs. Fox says she’ll never forget her doctor’s words: “Patricia, you’ll be a breast cancer survivor.” That sentiment set the tone for her mindset as a fighter. “It made me think that I could face this and survive this,” she says.

Still, cancer treatments rapidly overwhelmed Fox, and soon she faced her lowest point: crying on the floor for hours, feeling like having cancer at such a young age was a punishment for being a “bad person.” But she pulled herself out of it with hard work in therapy.

“I found that talking to a therapist helped me process my diagnosis and examine the areas of my life—certain people and my own behavior patterns—that were cancerous for me that I needed to do something about,” she states. “While therapy didn’t make the pain go away, it did make how I coped with it much better.”.

In the Black community, therapy is often taboo, claims Fox, but it’s become her mission to dispel that belief. “Therapy fortified me to get through cancer,” she says, “and I tell everyone that they don’t have to suffer in silence.”.

Annette Colden, 63, was sitting at her sister’s bedside during the last days of her final battle with breast cancer when the conversation turned to screenings. Her sister had been through cervical cancer and two bouts of breast cancer before passing away from the disease. “She made me promise I’d get my mammograms,” Colden states.

Colden’s first two yearly mammograms were clear. On the third there was a spot, but she was told by her doctor that things looked okay and it wasn’t cancer—she just had lumpy breasts.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s this inner feeling you have,” she states. “Something was inside me saying, That’s not right.” Her sister’s doctor had told her the exact same thing, but Colden was so happy to hear she didn’t have cancer that she didn’t follow up.

A year later she went back for a mammogram, and that’s when her doctors found it: stage 0 breast cancer, meaning only abnormal cells had been found. She was 42. “Now, looking back, I always tell women that if something doesn’t feel right, get a second opinion.”.

Despite the diagnosis Colden remained calm. “I’m a religious person,” she states. “In my prayer I remarked, ‘Lord, if you will be my pilot on this journey, I’ll be your copilot.’” She immediately felt a sense of peace.

In a recent development, after her recovery she decided to share that calming presence with other women going through breast cancer at a support group through Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, where she had treatment. “I say, ‘It’s going to be a long road. If you don’t want to travel it alone, I’m right there with you.’”.

It has been revealed that and she means it. Sometimes that involves talking with someone at 3 a.m. when the pain from chemotherapy hits. Other times it means sending food delivery boxes to the homes of people with breast cancer who can’t muster the strength to leave. “My sister did a lot of support work before she got really sick,” she says. “This is her vision.”.

It has been revealed that ricki Fairley, 69, was in the security line at the airport for a work trip when she got a call from her doctor. They’d found a peanut-like lump under her nipple that turned out to be cancer.

According to recent reports, fairley, who was 55 at the time, said, “I don’t have time for this right now. I’ll call you when I get to my destination.” A couple days later she found out she had stage 3A TNBC, and it was really aggressive. Compared with other breast cancers, TNBC has fewer targeted-therapy treatment options, often spreads beyond the breasts, and is more likely to recur. Black women have nearly three times the risk of developing triple-negative breast cancer.

Her diagnosis woke her up. “It made me realize that I needed to get all of the ‘cancers’ out of my life,” Fairley says. During treatment that first year which involved a double mastectomy, aggressive chemotherapy, and radiation, she quit her job and started her own tech giant. Then she filed for divorce and later sold her house. “I quit my life and started a newly introduced one, and changed everything,” she says. “I had to learn that my peace is nonnegotiable. I really think that stress caused my breast cancer.”.

A year later her life changed again. Fairley was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer and told she had two years to live. After finding out her current doctor had only treated two previous cases of TNBC and both women had died in eight months, she found a newly introduced doctor, who was well-versed in current research and treatments for the disease. She beat cancer a second time. “I remember sitting at my daughter’s graduation thinking, Okay, I made it. What’s next for me?” Fairley indicates. The answer: helping others. In the years that followed, Fairley cofounded The Black Breast Cancer Alliance, which works to reduce the mortality rate for Black women.

Are seed oils bad for you? Vegetable oil vs. olive oil vs. butter

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that from TikTok to bestseller lists, vegetable oils—a.k.a.
  • To be fair, folks have debated the merits of vegetable oils dating back to when they first entered the marketplace.
  • It has been revealed that more recently, however, with the advent of the carnivore diet, vegetable oil hate has roared back into the socials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that from TikTok to bestseller lists, vegetable oils—a.k.a. “seed oils”—are a substantial topic right now.

To be fair, folks have debated the merits of vegetable oils dating back to when they first entered the marketplace.

It has been revealed that more recently, however, with the advent of the carnivore diet, vegetable oil hate has roared back into the socials. Maybe you’ve come across posts that refer to these cooking oils as “toxic sludge,” “motor oil,” “the hateful eight,” and “the biggest cause of chronic disease that nobody knows about.”.

The anti-vegetable oil logic goes something like this….

Industry observers note that animal fats have been with humans for thousands of years. Vegetable fats, on the other hand, were invented during the last century when profit-seeking companies wanted to find a way to sell cheap-to-grow foods to unsuspecting consumers.

Another argument: Like margarine, vegetable oils were marketed as healthier alternatives for butter, and yet, people argue, these oils are worse than butter, raising your risk for obesity, anxiety, depression, ulcerative colitis, and more.

In contrast to the above line of thought, other experts will tell you that vegetable oils are harmless, potentially even health-promoting—and absolutely better than butter.

Like so many nutrition topics, the truth is too nuanced to fit on a meme.

In this story, we’ll help you sort the science from the pseudoscience so you can make informed decisions about the oils you choose to include in your diet.

According to recent reports, sometimes called “seed oils,” vegetable oils start, as you might suspect, from the seed of a plant. The most common ones you’ll find in a typical grocery aisle include:.

By the way, if you feel like there’s a bunch of oils missing from that list, it’s probably because those oils come from non-seed plants (such as olive, avocado, palm, or coconut oil, which all come from fruits, and aren’t considered vegetable or seed oils).

Non-vegetable oils—such as olive and avocado oil—are derived from naturally fatty foods. In fact, olives are so oily that you could theoretically make your own olive oil at home. (Just Google “how to make olive oil from scratch,” and you’ll find a number of videos walking you through the steps.).

The same can’t be mentioned of most vegetable oils, which mostly come from foods with a relatively tiny fat content to begin with.

Case in point: A cup of green olives contains about 20 grams of fat,1 whereas a cup of corn has 2 grams.2.

In a recent development, as a result, manufacturers must use an extensive multi-step process to extract this small amount of oil from these non-oily foods. These steps include:.

During this process, health-promoting polyphenols and other stabilizing nutrients are lost, and small amounts of unsaturated fats are transformed into trans fatty acids (also called partially hydrogenated fat).

(Interesting fact: This also happens during deep frying. When vegetable oils sizzle in a restaurant’s deep fryer for hours, the trans fat content of the oil increases.).

Industry observers note that to call these processed oils “toxic” might be an exaggeration. However, nutrition scientists generally agree that people should avoid trans fats in the diet, and in 2018, the Food and Drug Administration banned manufacturers from adding trans fats to processed foods.3 4.

At PN, we’ve created several visual guides people can use to make informed decisions about what to eat.

Sources indicate that (We’ve also created a shopping list, which you or your clients can print out and take to the grocery store. Check it out: Healthy Fats Shopping List).

In these guides, we’ve placed a few vegetable oils—expeller-pressed canola oil, high-oleic sunflower, and safflower oils—in the “Eat Some” section. For us, “eat some” is another way of saying that these foods will neither improve health nor harm health—when consumed in reasonable amounts. In some cases, like in the example of dark chocolate, when consumed in small amounts, they might even improve health.

The rest of the vegetable oils, along with butter and other saturated fats, fall into the “Eat Less” category, as the image below reveals. You’ll find vegetable oils in bold.

We’ve gotten hate mail from folks who say certain vegetable oils—especially cold-pressed canola oil—should appear alongside olive oil in the “eat more” category. Plenty of others say all vegetable oils belong in the “eat less” column, and that butter belongs in “eat some” or even “eat more.”.

To understand the scientific reasoning behind our recommendations, let’s explore some head-to-head matchups.

These oils are the least refined of their kind.

To make extra virgin olive oil (EVOO), manufacturers grind and mechanically press olives, without using any heat. Similarly, expeller-pressed canola oil is made by mechanically pressing rapeseed, without the use of heat or chemical solvents.

Olive oil is richer in heart-healthy monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) than almost any other cooking oil.

Industry observers note that in addition, unlike the more refined “light” olive oil, EVOO maintains most of the olive fruit’s original polyphenols. These plant-based substances help to combat inflammation and protect cells from damage.

More studies vouch for EVOO’s health-promoting qualities than for any other cooking fat.

It has been revealed that for example, researchers asked 22,892 adults from Southern Italy to self-report their olive oil consumption. People who consumed the most olive oil (more than two tablespoons a day) were 20 percent less likely to die over the 13-year study than people who consumed the least olive oil (less than one tablespoon a day).5.

Other research has linked the consumption of olive oil with a reduced risk of:.

Consumption of olive oil is also associated with reductions in LDL cholesterol, especially when used to replace saturated fats like butter and coconut oil.10.

Years ago, culinary experts recommended using EVOO only on salads and other uncooked foods. Back then, they assumed EVOO’s relatively low smoke point (350 to 410F) meant the oil would break down when heated, losing some of its distinctive flavor and health benefits.

We now know that smoke point isn’t as massive a deal as previously thought.

That’s especially true in the case of EVOO, whose polyphenols and high concentrations of monounsaturated fats help keep the oil stable when heated.

In research that heated a variety of cooking oils to 464 F (240C) and then held them at 356 F (180C) for several hours, EVOO remained more stable than any other oil tested, including canola oil.11.

One of the more affordable cooking oils on the shelf, canola oil, is made from a Canadian-made hybrid of the rapeseed plant.

(The word “canola” refers to the first three letters of “Canada” with a fun “ola” added to the end for marketing purposes.)12.

Among vegetable oils, canola is the richest in heart-healthy monounsaturated fats (though several non-vegetable oils have it beat) as well as alpha-linolenic acid, a plant-based omega-3 fatty acid.

In addition, canola oil contains plant substances called phytosterols that help influence blood cholesterol for the better, especially when used as a substitute for butter, research has found.13 14 15.

Extra virgin olive oil is the clear winner.

The body of research in support of EVOO dwarfs the body of research in support of expeller-pressed canola.

Industry observers note that in addition, EVOO has a more favorable fatty acid profile. By the way, so does avocado oil, which is why you’ll also find it in the “eat more” column.

However, you can buy roughly twice as much expeller-pressed canola oil for half as much money as EVOO. Because of this, expeller-pressed canola can be a good budget-friendly choice. In addition, because of expeller-pressed canola’s more neutral flavor, many people prefer it over EVOO for baking.

When used in moderation, expeller-pressed canola can be part of a healthy diet. It is likely to be at least health neutral, if not somewhat health beneficial.

This match-up comes down to how processing methods affect the end product.

An expeller press is a machine that squeezes oil out of seeds.

It’s able to do this without the use of solvents or heat, which helps preserve beneficial compounds such as alpha-linolenic acid and phytosterols.

Refining removes some protective alpha-linoleic acid while adding small amounts of unhealthy trans fatty acids. This results in a product that is proportionally lower in omega-3 fatty acids and higher in omega-6 fatty acids.

Expeller-pressed canola oil wins, but only by a small margin.

Industry observers note that that’s because canola oil starts with a less controversial fatty acid profile than many other vegetable oils, as the chart below shows. Soybean oil, for example, has less heart-healthy monounsaturated fat and much more theoretically inflammation-contributing omega-6 fat.

The typical American consumes around 16 to 20 times more omega-6 fats than omega-3s.

This imbalance could theoretically increase inflammation in your body, potentially raising your risk for diabetes, obesity, and other health problems, argue some experts.16.

It has been revealed that years ago, the recommendation to balance your omega 6s with omega 3s was widespread. (The suggested “ideal” ratio: Anywhere from 1:1 to 4:1, in favor of omega 6s.).

These days, there’s more debate among nutritional scientists as to whether this imbalance contributes to chronic inflammation, especially when those omega 6s are consumed in whole foods that contain many other beneficial compounds.

For example, nuts and seeds—both naturally rich in omega-6 fats—have been associated with a range of health benefits, including reductions in blood cholesterol and inflammation.17 18.

In 2019, Harvard Health ran the headline “No need to avoid healthy omega-6 fats.” In support of their argument, a 2019 study from the American Heart Association journal Circulation determined that, if anything, the consumption of omega-6 fats reduced the risk for stroke, heart disease, and early death.19.

However, while nuts and refined canola oil may share a somewhat similar fatty acid profile, the two foods differ in one important way. As we mentioned earlier, refined canola oil is basically pure oil. Meanwhile, nuts and seeds come packaged with health-protective fiber, polyphenols, protein, vitamins, and minerals.

Minimally-processed foods, like nuts or extra virgin oils, include a complex matrix of health-promoting nutrients. Highly-processed oils, on the other hand, have lost the vast majority of those healthful compounds, leaving mostly just the fatty acids which are more prone to oxidation (we’ll cover that next).

This is the match-up that triggers the most arguing on the interwebs.

Let’s cover the major claims from both sides—plus what the research says.

Butter proponents argue that saturated fats have been unnecessarily vilified. They point to nutrition recommendations during the 1980s and 1990s that recommended people replace butter with trans-fat rich margarine.

Margarine aside, others claim the research in support of reducing saturated fats is thin at best.20.

However, excessive saturated fat consumption (beyond 10 percent of total calories) does seem to boost cholesterol levels and may increase your risk of heart disease.21.

Some research has found that replacing 5 percent of the saturated fats in your diet with monounsaturated fats could reduce the risk of heart disease by 15 percent. Similarly, replacing 5 percent of the saturated fats in your diet with polyunsaturated fats (with most of that coming from refined vegetable oils) reduces the risk of a future heart attack by 10 percent, according to an analysis of eight studies involving 13,614 people.22 Many other studies support this finding.23.

It has been revealed that but not all saturated fats affect blood cholesterol equally. In some dairy foods, a membrane—called a milk fat globule membrane—surrounds the saturated fats and seems to limit their cholesterol-raising properties.

However, butter is low in this protective membrane, and consequently raises blood cholesterol more than other high-fat dairy products, like full-fat milk, cream, yogurt, or cheese.24 25 26.

Industry observers note that the U.S. Dietary Guidelines recommend capping saturated fat at less than 10 percent of your calorie intake. A tablespoon of butter contains 7 grams of saturated fat—a third of the recommended daily limit in a 2000 Calorie diet.

So, while you don’t necessarily need to eliminate butter, it’s worth moderating your intake.

(Interested in learning about all the nuances of saturated fat consumption? Read: Is saturated fat good or bad for you?).

Due to their chemical structure, polyunsaturated fats are inherently less stable and more prone to oxidation than saturated or monounsaturated fats.

According to recent reports, during the refining process, protective phytochemicals and antioxidants are stripped, making these oils more prone to oxidation. The theory is that this oxidation increases inflammation in the body and elevates the risk of various health conditions.

There’s some evidence to suggest that diets rich in polyunsaturated fats, especially from refined vegetable oils, are associated with increased levels of oxidized blood lipids, lipid peroxidation, and other markers of inflammation.27 28.

If you only use refined corn or safflower oils to lightly coat veggies before roasting them, you likely don’t have much to worry about.

However, for the vast majority of people, the biggest source of refined vegetable oils isn’t home-cooked meals—it’s ultra-processed foods.

It has been revealed that the extra processing and repeated heat exposure used to create ultra-processed foods further oxidize these oils. Additionally, these foods are often loaded with potentially harmful ingredients like added sodium and sugars, and low in beneficial nutrients like fiber, vitamins, minerals, and phytonutrients.

It has been revealed that plus, they’re incredibly calorie-dense and difficult to stop eating, which can raise your risk for obesity. (Find out exactly why highly-processed foods are so “addictive”: Why you can’t stop eating ultra-processed foods.).

In a large review involving nearly 10 million people, the consumption of ultra-processed foods was associated with a higher risk of premature death.29 In addition, studies have linked high consumption of ultra-processed foods with the following health problems:30 31 32 33.

You don’t have to abolish ultra-processed foods.

But your health will benefit from capping your consumption to about 20 percent or so of your intake, with the other 80 percent or so from mostly minimally-processed whole foods.

This alone will naturally lower your refined vegetable oil intake to a safer level, without much fuss. Plus, consuming refined vegetable oils in the context of a diet that’s rich in colorful plants, fiber, phytochemicals, and antioxidants may help offset the concern of oxidation. (For example, by putting a reasonable amount of commercial salad dressing on a large, colorful salad.).

Ultimately, both should be limited in the diet, and neither are health-promoting.

Industry observers note that most refined vegetable oils are lopsidedly rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids compared to monounsaturated fats, and are stripped of many protective compounds. As mentioned earlier, some experts argue that these omega-6-rich fats may contribute to inflammation (but the evidence here is mixed). Because of how they’re processed, seed oils also contain some of those trans fats that everyone agrees we should all minimize.

In contrast, butter is low in omega 6s but high in saturated fat, which can be problematic in higher amounts. Especially since it’s so low in the protective milk fat globule membrane. However, compared to refined vegetable oil, butter is less processed. Like olive oil, it’s one of those fats you could theoretically make at home.

This might be obvious from the head-to-head matchups, but we’ll say it anyway.

If you like it and can afford it, EVOO is a great choice.

Cold-pressed avocado oil and walnut oil are also great options, as both are rich in antioxidant compounds. Like EVOO, avocado oil is a rich source of MUFAs. Walnut oil’s fat primarily comes from polyunsaturated fats, so it’s best used as a dressing rather than used for cooking (as it’s less heat stable).

Industry observers note that however, like EVOO, avocado and walnut oil tend to be expensive. If you or your client are budget-conscious, expeller-pressed canola oil is a solid runner-up.

It has been revealed that similarly, high-oleic sunflower and safflower oils are richer sources of monounsaturated fats than their high-linoleic cousins. When substituted for saturated fats like butter, high-oleic oils have been associated with cardiovascular benefits.34 35.

Regardless of what cooking fats you or your client choose, you’ll also want to do the following:.

Recent findings suggest that whole and minimally-processed foods—such as nuts, seeds, avocados, olives, and salmon—are more likely to feature health-promoting monounsaturated (MUFAs) and omega-3 fats. They also come packaged with a wide array of other good-for-you nutrients such as fiber, protein, minerals, and antioxidants.

It has been revealed that in contrast, ultra-professed foods are generally devoid of everything you keep hearing you should consume more of. These foods also tend to be calorie-dense, highly rewarding, and hard to stop eating.

If you’re not sure whether packaged food is minimally processed or highly processed, take a close look and consider:.

If you answer “no” to most of the above, the food is likely highly processed.

It doesn’t matter what source of fat is used to fry them.

Sort all fried foods into the “eat less” category.

It has been revealed that EVOO is associated with longer, healthier lives. However, that doesn’t mean you should be doing shots of it.

As a general rule, you’re better off getting most of your fat from foods like avocados, olives, nuts and seeds than from any cooking oil.

Industry observers note that whole food fats are rich in fiber, phytochemicals, vitamins, and minerals, and are generally less calorie-dense than oils. (But having one to three servings of oils or butter per day is reasonable.).

Industry News: Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.
  • You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.
  • Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

Industry observers note that A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:.

In a recent development, that hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

Your body doesn’t have a cutoff age.

According to recent reports, people in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

Sources indicate that as a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

According to recent reports, that’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.).

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:.

Is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

It has been revealed that but the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

According to recent reports, you’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Recent findings suggest that try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!).

Sources indicate that grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a new skill.

2) It takes way less than you think.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

Recent findings suggest that you can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down.

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

If you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Becky, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, is someone I immediately thought of when I read that initial email. She’s 77, and didn’t start going to the gym until she was 57. Here’s what she had to say:.

Sources indicate that I couldn’t have stated it any better myself, Becky. 😊.

No matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪.
