SHOP GARMIN DEALS ON AMAZON SHOP DEALS ON GARMIN.COM.

Garmin GPS head units are one of the smartest upgrades you can make to your road, gravel, mountain, or electric bike, and a much safer alternative than strapping your phone to the bars to see your route. Cycling computers also capture, process, and display data from accessories like heart rate monitors, power meters, and even electronic shifting to help you ride better, train smarter, and stay connected. And because Garmin lets you customize nearly everything—from data fields to navigation screens—you can tailor exactly what reveals up.

It has been revealed that buying Tip: Buying previous-generation cycling computers is a great way to save money. Older models usually have almost the same performance at a big discount. Cyclists often even prefer the old models if they’re lighterweight or have better battery life.

Cycling radar is one of the most vital pieces of bicycle technology released in the last decade. On-bike radar systems mount to the rear of your bike and feature an integrated taillight. Paired with a cycling computer or smartwatch, they notify you about vehicles approaching from behind so you can move out of the way. They are a must-have item for road and gravel riders.

It has been revealed that buying Tip: Garmin is a pioneer in cycling radar tech and makes the most reliable, consistent systems. The Varia RTL515 is our benchmark and best-value pick, while the RearVue 820 is newer and more powerful; it’s our choice for best performance. The RCT715 is the 515 with an integrated rear-facing camera.

It has been revealed that while dedicated cycling computers are the go-to choice for road, gravel, and data-heavy training, many riders prefer Garmin’s smartwatches because they keep everything in one place, especially when they track more than bike rides—anyone who mixes riding with running, hiking, paddling, strength training, or even walking the dog. Garmin watches have powerful GPS, workout metrics, and daily health data in a streamlined device that’s always with you (and they even tell time).

Recent findings suggest that buying Tip: Mountain bikers often appreciate the simplicity and safety of recording their rides from the wrist rather than risking a pricey head unit in a crash. Triathletes, duathletes, and cyclocross racers love the seamless transitions a watch allows. There’s no need to swap devices or merge files after an event.

According to recent reports, most riders know Garmin from its computers, smartwatches, and cycling radar. But Garmin also owns the indoor trainer brand Tacx. Its smart trainers and indoor bikes are highly regarded for their excellent performance, integration, and useful features. One cool feature we love—especially if you live somewhere prone to winter power outages—is that the Neo 2T generates its own resistance electromagnetically. That means you don’t have to scrap your workout plans just because the lights go out.

Buying Tip: Smart trainers are great for riding in virtual worlds like Zwift. For a deep dive into more great indoor trainers and buying info, check out my story “Ready to Ride Indoors? Here’s How to Pick the Best Trainer.”.

Power pedals, like Garmin’s Rally series, are easier to install than crank-based power meter options. Plus, you can swap power pedals easily between bikes. This not only saves cost, but it also gives you consistent data from bike to bike.

Industry observers note that buying Tip: Garmin offers a handy option to buy its power meter in a package including two pedal styles (road and mountain bike/gravel) with swappable spindles. This way you can measure power across riding disciplines.

  • In a recent development, there was a time when you could spot someone who had just finished a run.
  • Running shoes have officially entered their fashion era, and while the whole sneaker-meets-streetwear thing isn't exactly newly introduced (the chunky dad sneaker era still lives rent-free in my head), the latest wave of collaborations feels a little different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, there was a time when you could spot someone who had just finished a run. They were sweaty and wearing sneakers that looked like they belonged exclusively on a track. These days, the shoes tell you almost nothing. That guy wearing carbon-plated racers might be heading out for a tempo run, or he might just be on his way to a bar or running errands (in a casual fit).

Running shoes have officially entered their fashion era, and while the whole sneaker-meets-streetwear thing isn't exactly newly introduced (the chunky dad sneaker era still lives rent-free in my head), the latest wave of collaborations feels a little different. Instead of reviving old silhouettes, fashion brands are getting their hands on actual performance shoes, and, frankly, some of the results are pretty damn good.

Take Adidas' collaboration with Satisfy, the Parisian running brand that's become something of a cult favorite among runners who lowkey like to look good while out and about. Earlier this year, the two brands gave the Adizero Adios Pro 4 a makeover, swapping its usual racing aesthetic for earthy tones, spray-painted details, and metallic accents. At first glance, they look like something you could spot on an edgy Instagram campaign, perhaps even a fashion week after-party in Bushwick, depending on the outfit. Except, it's still a legitimate racing shoe with Lightstrike Pro foam and EnergyRods. You could absolutely chase a PR in these. Whether you'd want to get them dirty is another question. That’s just merely scraping the surface, though.

In a recent development, highsnobiety's latest collaboration with Saucony takes a similar approach, but with two very different sneakers: the Endorphin Pro 5, made for racing, and the ProGrid Paramount, a retro-inspired shoe that's more at home on city streets. Both get a modest makeover that makes technical sneakers look good with practically anything. Some of you probably appreciate the distinction here: one shoe is built for runners, and the other is for people who strictly care about style.

According to recent reports, then there's Hoka x Marni, which might be one of my favorites of the bunch. After giving the Bondi a ridiculously puffy, almost cartoonish makeover in 2025, the brands returned this November with the Clifton Marni, a more wearable take on Hoka's Clifton 11. There are metallic details, reflective accents, and a plaid sockliner, but underneath it all is still the cushioned daily trainer runners already know. It's stylish without looking like it's trying too hard, which can't be noted for every designer sneaker collaboration.

Industry observers note that other brands have been getting in on the fun, too. Salomon and Pas Normal Studios recently put their spin on the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL, giving the gravel running shoe a sleek, outdoorsy look while keeping its GORE-TEX protection and trail-ready outsole. Aimé Leon Dore has brought its signature Newly introduced York aesthetic to New Balance's FuelCell Rebel v5 and SC Elite v5, while Nike tapped designer Melitta Baumeister to reimagine the Vomero Premium and Pegasus Premium. Even Loewe and On are experimenting with high-fashion versions of technical running shoes. By now, the crossover is hard to ignore.

Industry observers note that of course, there's something funny about running, a sport that really doesn't require much beyond a decent pair of shoes (and your ability to actually run, of course), becoming another excuse to buy expensive, limited-edition sneakers. And not that this has to be noted, but a designer collaboration isn't automatically a better running shoe. The fit, cushioning, and performance still matter, especially if you're planning to do more than walk around in them. But I do think it's cool that brands are putting this much thought into how performance footwear looks. Running clothes have gotten a lot more stylish in recent years, so why shouldn't the shoes follow?

Josiah Soto is a commerce editor and writer at Hearst Magazines, where he covers skincare, grooming, beauty, and style for Men’s Health, Prevention, and BestProducts.com. With a particular passion for skincare and the ingredients behind his favorite products, he keeps readers up to date on the latest beauty launches, grooming essentials, and fashion trends worth knowing about. He also contributes to Runner’s World and Popular Mechanics, covering everything from emerging style trends to running gear and lifestyle products. In another life, Josiah was an editor at ThePioneerWoman.com.

Canyon’s PACE Cockpit Has a Clever Answer to One of Integrated Bars’ Biggest Problems

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Integrated cockpits can be light, aerodynamic, and good-looking.
  • It has been revealed that I’ve given Canyon’s PACE system plenty of criticism in my reviews.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Integrated cockpits can be light, aerodynamic, and good-looking. They can also make simple jobs harder than they need to be. Adjusting your position can mean cutting a steerer tube. Replacing a broken handlebar can mean buying a whole new cockpit. And routing brake hoses through everything can turn a small change into a long afternoon.

It has been revealed that I’ve given Canyon’s PACE system plenty of criticism in my reviews. It’s proprietary, and integrated systems come with real compromises. But after swapping the drops on the Endurace CF SLX 9 I have in for review, I want to give Canyon credit for a thoughtful design choice.

Sources indicate that the main section of the PACE cockpit is called the T-Bar. Canyon’s system lets you adjust cockpit height by up to 20 mm in 5mm increments, without cutting the steerer. The cockpit is also made up of three pieces, with the drop sections bolted to the T-Bar. That offers a couple of advantages.

First, it makes the bar width adjustable. The T-Bar has three width positions, 25 mm apart, for a total range of 50 mm. The actual widths depend on the drop shape. See the table below.

In a recent development, the bolt-on drops also let Canyon offer five shapes with different dimensions. If the drops that come on your new Canyon don’t suit you, you can swap them for another option.

Recent findings suggest that my Endurace review bike came with the Compact drops. They have a 108mm drop, width settings from 390 to 440 mm, and 8 degrees of flare. I prefer a narrower bar with a deeper drop and more flare, so I switched to Canyon’s Control drops. They have a 120mm drop, adjust from 370 to 420 mm, and feature 17 degrees of flare.

*U.S. prices at the time of writing. Bar tape and fixing screws are included.

Sources indicate that here’s what I needed to do to make the swap: unwrap the bar, loosen and slide off the controls, remove the old drops, install the fresh ones, then tighten everything and rewrap the bar. Canyon includes fresh bar tape with the replacement drops.

Canyon also includes a clever cardboard tool that helps you evenly align your controls. I loved it!

With most one-piece integrated cockpits, switching to a different bar shape or replacing a broken drop means replacing the whole assembly. Depending on the bike’s routing, that may also mean disconnecting or replacing brake hoses and bleeding the brakes.

It has been revealed that on the PACE, the brake hoses run behind the drop sections rather than through them, so I didn’t have to disconnect or cut them. That meant no brake bleed, no risk of ending up with a hose that’s too short, and no replacing the entire cockpit.

It has been revealed that that also matters if you crash and break a drop. With a one-piece handlebar and stem, a broken bar can mean replacing the whole assembly. With PACE, you can replace the damaged section.*.

*If you break a drop, check the PACE T-Bar, or stem, for damage, too. Replace it if necessary.

Industry observers note that the system can also make bike travel less nerve-racking. If your bar tape is set up so the controls can slide on and off without rewrapping, you can unbolt the drops and let them hang out of the way. The bike packs a little narrower, and the handlebar ends are less exposed to side impacts. I’ve had bars damaged in transit more times than I can count, so I appreciate this feature.

PACE is still proprietary, and those concerns don’t disappear because one part of the system is clever. But integrated cockpits often force riders to accept limited adjustability, few shape options, and costly replacements. Canyon has found a useful way to make its handlebar easier to fit, repair, and travel with. For that, it deserves some credit.

Industry observers note that A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

After 3 Marathons Without a Plan, I Finally Followed One. Here’s What Happened in NYC.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the first time I entered the Fresh York City Marathon drawing, I got in.
  • Sources indicate that my NYC Marathon training also happened during my senior year of college, which brought its own challenges.
  • While training for those first few marathons, I didn’t have any real plan, except to not let it interfere with my social calendar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the first time I entered the Fresh York City Marathon drawing, I got in. I’m not sure what possessed me that day to apply, having never run another race in my life. I figured I’d never get in, so why not? I played soccer growing up, and when the world shut down during COVID-19, running became the easiest way to get out of the house and see my friends. That’s where my running journey began.

Sources indicate that my NYC Marathon training also happened during my senior year of college, which brought its own challenges. While I was excited to run, I also didn’t want to miss out on any of the socializing that happened that year. I did my best to make it to every party, every club soccer game, and anything in between while running as much as possible. I was scared that running was going to infringe on my everyday life and I wouldn’t have time to keep having fun. Despite all of that, I had caught the marathon bug and after finishing the Upcoming York City Marathon in 2022, I went on to run the Paris and Chicago Marathons in 2024.

While training for those first few marathons, I didn’t have any real plan, except to not let it interfere with my social calendar. My strategy consisted of building up mileage in order to reach 20 miles about four weeks out from race day. In between, I pieced together training information from influencers on Instagram and Google searches (this was pre-ChatGPT!). Now that I’m a Runner’s World+ member, I have all those resources right at my fingertips.

Although I caught the marathon bug almost instantly, I also felt defeated after Newly introduced York. I knew I could have done better. Between New York City in 2022 and Paris in 2024, I never ran more than 10 miles at a time, but I was running enough that I knew I could do it again if I really wanted. I followed a similar approach for Chicago in 2024: Build up to one long run about a month out, then fill the rest of the weeks with shorter runs and one medium-length run. It wasn’t much of a plan, but it worked for me. My times kept improving, and I broke four hours for the first time in Chicago.

According to recent reports, looking back, I realize that my no-proposal approach was partly a way to protect myself. If I never mentioned my goal out loud, I couldn’t feel disappointed if I missed it. Breaking four hours in Chicago changed that. For the first time, I wanted to see what I could do with a real plan.

Industry observers note that I was now living in the city I had expected to call home ever since I left college, so I really wanted this race to feel meaningful. For the first time in my marathon career, I downloaded a Runner’s World training plan, the 16-week Break 3:45 plan to be exact, printed it out, and started tracking all of my runs. I wanted to beat my time in Chicago and get as close to 3 hours and 45 minutes as possible.

In a recent development, in the beginning, this felt super daunting. I had never done an interval run in my life nor had I ever intentionally sought out hills to make my runs feel harder than they already did. Nonetheless, I found my old Garmin Forerunner 55 and learned how to upload intervals to run up and down the West Side Highway. When the plan called for hills, I made my way back to the Queensboro Bridge for the first time since 2022, ready to face it with excitement instead of fear. Even while pretending to be excited, the incline is no joke!

For a while, I really felt like I had gotten the hang of things. I actually started to recognize what different paces felt like during the intervals, instead of sprinting and pulling back and looking at my watch while I ran. And, I could now confidently run over many of the bridges in New York City, notably the Williamsburg and Manhattan, even though they aren’t even part of the marathon course. I wasn’t following the proposal exactly, but I was able to reorganize the days of the week to hit all the workouts.

According to recent reports, this was working! Until it wasn’t.

Near the end of August (roughly week eight of the plan), it became hot all the time, I was constantly traveling for weekend trips, and I had started to lose the excitement of running. So while I was making sure to hit all of the long runs, the interval training fell off completely. I was a little disappointed in myself because the interval training runs were workouts that made me feel like I was getting stronger each week. I had never done this type of workout before, so I could tell I was getting better each time.

In a recent development, to find the joy of running again, I really started to lean on my friends. Every week, I’d send out a few texts to see who was available and wanted to go for a run with me. I ran the loop in Central Park almost every week and met up with my friends in Brooklyn to run every Friday morning. I started to explore parts of the city I had never been to before, which helped ground me in my training and remember that running is supposed to be fun and is an exciting way to explore the city.

From my previous experience, I knew that running the long runs was the most important thing for me to feel confident on race day. So much of marathon running is mental, so knowing that I could run 20 miles (and have run 26.2 before), was enough for me. So, while I started with a proposal, I started reverting back to my tried-and-true method—the just make sure you run the long runs plan.

Sources indicate that outside of the training plan itself, I leaned on Runner’s World a lot. I didn’t have access to this in the past so I didn’t feel confident about planning for prerun meals or even how to take gels during the race. I also found that being able to read runner stories online made me feel more connected to the community, which helped me mentally with my training.

Blueprint or no plan, I’m proud of myself! My official time was 3:57:39, so while I did not achieve my goal of breaking 3:45, I did run a sub-4 race, and following the Runner’s World plan helped me get there. The last time I ran this race, I was a senior in college and thought I had it all figured out. I was going to move to New York City, get a real adult job, and start the life I had been imagining. Similar to my experience following the Runner’s World plan, this is not how everything went. Instead, I moved to a different city after graduating, eventually found my way back to New York, and my life is so much more full than I ever expected because of it. Maybe things aren’t always supposed to go to plan, and that’s a good thing!

#22286. Industry News: The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3899 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • There are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here.
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here. There’s also a slew of latest super shoes that made their debut this marathon cycle. We’ll update accordingly once these racers are available.

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use). Today, almost every shoe brand has a super shoe with a carbon plate and super foams, and they all make the same promise as the Vaporfly 4%: less energy expenditure while racing, or the ability to run faster with the same effort.

Here, we list the top performers based on wear-tester feedback and our own experiences racing in them. And if you’re in the market for other shoes to help you with your training, we have a buying guide for those too.

Your first marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)For a PR → Nike Alphafly 4 (Men’s/Women’s)But want to train in a plated shoe → New Balance SC Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)A flat and fast course → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 (Unisex)A half marathon → Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo (Unisex)And want to try low drop → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)And need support → Saucony Endorphin Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)And have wide feet → Hoka Cielo X1 3.0 (Unisex)On a track → Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 (Men’s/Women’s)A 5K or 10K → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)On a trail → Hoka Tecton X 4 (Men’s/Women’s)An ultra → On Cloudultra Pro (Men’s/Women’s).

Recent findings suggest that besides our local testers, some of whom have been testing for us for the past 15 years, and staff who’ve also logged their share of road and trail time in these shoes, I have tested several of these shoes on race days. I have run 28 marathons since 2010, including 14 consecutive Boston Marathons. And I have made the split-second decision to race in upcoming shoes marathon morning.

Industry observers note that I’ve spoken with brand shoe development teams and have kept up with the latest super shoe releases. Fresh shoes not listed here are still undergoing the testing process and will be added once feedback is in.

All of the shoes on this list were tested by local runners and Runner’s World staff. Our local testers include 300-plus men and women of various running experience levels, paces, arch heights, and gait patterns. From enthusiasts who run for fun to several Olympic-qualifying hopefuls, our mix of testers rounds out a sample of the overall running pop.

Recent findings suggest that RW editors, including myself, have also raced in these shoes, from 5K to marathon distance (and some ultrarunners). We take into consideration fit, feel, and ride to determine the best racing shoes for almost every kind of runner hoping to PR, or just enjoy the propulsive experience of running on carbon plates sandwiched between super foams.

Sources indicate that on a plane, running a shakeout run, and anytime a marathon was weeks away or days past, I’d hear first-timers and seasoned vets say the Adizero Adios Pro 4 was their race day shoe of choice. The latest iteration is sure to have the same mentions next race cycle.

I didn’t have the chance to race in the Adizero Adios Pro 5 yet, but I did try them out on my usual Central Park circuit in New York City. I was practically racing my casual loop after slurping half a can of beer (it was a long day on the job). It obviously wasn’t the kiwi-flavored Belgian White that had me clocking marathon pace (it got kinda funky after the 25th sip).

The carbon rim, which replaces the 4’s energy rods, is the secret sauce that subtracts weights and encourages a powerful snap that had me run up and down Harlem Hill like a gazelle. The Lightstrike Pro foam is also slightly firmer, which helps with high rebound and stability.

Recent findings suggest that my only knock is how the rim shreds the hell of my ankle if my form gets slow and sloppy. But it’s a character trait. Senior Art Director Colin McSherry, for instance, ran his first marathon and had no problems—shoe- or first 26.2-related—during his run.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com.

Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review.

The Alphafly 3 went through some major changes to become more inclusive in terms of fit, weight, and ride. How do you upgrade a shoe that was worn by the late Kelvin Kiptum, former marathon world record holder (2:00:35)? It starts with the Air units.

The ones in the Alphafly 4 are lighter and softer. During his testing, Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes down when you stomp on the forefoot. The effect is a smoother, comfier ride with lots of pop.

The width of the shoe is also slightly wider (Nike really wants runners to stop saying their shoes are too unstable and narrow). Dengate noted how he didn’t have to slow down when turning corners.

The main critique is that loud clomping sound. But at this point—is it really an Alphafly if you can’t hear it coming up from behind you meters away?

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Industry observers note that the jury is still out on the pros and cons of solely training in super shoes, but we’re in the camp of keeping your special trainer fresh for race day. You can get a couple of runs in to troubleshoot and see if there are any challenges pre-marathon or half, but I still urge runners to save the magic. But if you can’t get enough of that super foam, carbon plate high, enter the SC Rebel.

New Balance created this shoe specifically to make your training feel easier. It has the brand’s new TPEE-based Infinion foam, tuned for power runs, just like the SuperComp Elite v6 (New Balance’s premium racing shoe). It’s also an ideal alternative for racing if you need more stability. The shoe has a broader platform and grippy outsole that kept me upright on wet mud during a long run.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Latest Balance SuperComp Rebel Review.

It has been revealed that the Endorphin Elite 3 is as squishy and bouncy as its predecessor, but Saucony made the shoe more stable by connecting the forefoot and heel. Turns are less scary, but there’s still a learning curve to master the incredible energy return running in these shoes.

I tested them at a 5K and 3K in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, which was pocked with potholes and patched with slippery gravel. The shoes cut corners, but I still felt the need to slow down—or wipe out. I think on a more controlled runner’s feet these would make her feel powerful and unbeatable.

The source of that aggressive bounce is the TPEE-based IncrediRun foam. Its ride rivals even PEBA’s energy return.

The shoe also didn’t produce hot spots in the toe area. Saucony seems to have improved the fit with the third version. Once I wield this shoe’s power I won’t be afraid to run longer than a 10K. No friction here.

Shop Endorphin Elite 3 at saucony.com.

Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 Review.

When I ran the Tokyo Marathon last year, I laced up in the Asics Metaspeed Sky Paris because I wanted more cushioning in the forefoot area. Asics recognized there are two ways of racing: stride running or cadence running. The Sky is intended for stride running: when you have a more powerful gait with longer strides and tend to strike on the midfoot.

Sources indicate that at the Sydney Marathon this year, I opted for the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo instead. I felt the Edge would give me the, er, competitive edge, so to speak. My steps per minute are usually more than the average runner due to my mechanics and, well, because I’m short. The shoe has a scooped plate tilted slightly downward to cater to those with shorter steps (cadence running). I ended up hitting my sub-3:10 goal, finishing in 3:05.

The Edge Tokyo is updated with a softer underfoot, making the shoe more flexible. This makes the shoe have an incredible snap at toe-off. I was able to change gears at a fast clip when I latched onto a runner I was determined to pass (not always the best race strategy, but worked like a charm when I saw male runners try to overtake me).

Sources indicate that where competitors’ shoes have “air pods” or decoupled heels, the Metaspeeds provide runners with a simplified, choose-your-own-adventure super shoe that packs a powerful punch. One note for the wise: Because the Edge Tokyo has less firm cushioning, my heels and arches felt sore postrace. If you have heavy footfalls like me, have those recovery sandals waiting for you at bag check.

Shop Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at amazon.com.

Asics Metaspeed Tokyo Shoes Review.

Altra started its journey into super shoes by staying true to itself. The Vanish Carbon 1 and 2 had wide toeboxes and were zero drop. But the Altra team knew there would have to be a compromise to go up against competitors’ shoes: the Vanish Carbon 3 needed a drop. The brand preserved the Altra way by adding just 4 mm (like the shoes in its Experience collection) to the heel with an aggressive rocker profile to promote propulsion.

Another Altra signature in the shoe is the roomy toebox that gives racers space to splay their toes, allowing them to engage their digits and power up during push-off.

Sources indicate that the third iteration has pure PEBA midsole foam called FastRce. The foam provides more energy return and 2.6 percent improved running economy over the Vanish Carbon 2, which had a PEBA/EVA blend in its midsole.

The overall package presents a racer capable of racing against the other super shoes on this list.

Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

The Endorphin Pro 5 has a more stable ride than its springier sibling, the Endorphin Elite 2, which we also included on this list.

Industry observers note that its midsole is dual-layer PEBA, with one layer Pwrrun PB and the other layer Pwrrun HG. These layers provide a high-rebound ride and work with the rocker Speedroll tech to encourage fast, smooth turnover.

Testers like the shoe’s propulsive ride as well as support throughout their workouts.

“What stood out most was the combination of propulsion and stability,” said tester Srah Pezzino. “The carbon plate paired with Saucony’s Pwrrun HG foam delivers a responsive, fast ride without feeling unstable or overly bouncy. This helped immensely during longer tempo runs when fatigue starts to creep in. I felt like the shoe encouraged good mechanics and smooth turnover rather than forcing speed.

“Compared to previous carbon-plated shoes I’ve worn, the Pro 5 feels more predictable and controlled, especially when my form isn’t perfect late in a run. It’s a shoe that makes you feel fast without punishing you for not being perfectly locked in.”.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

Recent findings suggest that the lightest Hoka marathon racing shoe yet is the Cielo X1 3.0, with street cred at the 2025 Chicago Marathon. Hoka-sponsored pro-runner Alex Masai raced in a blacked-out prototype of the shoe, shaved nearly four minutes off his personal best time, and podiumed third with a 2:04:37 finish.

And our testers clocked the shoe’s massive updates, as well. “The 3.0 is sturdier than the 2.0,” said tester Mike Browne. “I’m referring to the sturdiness mainly on heel strikes. I wore the 2.0 during marathon training and in a marathon, and they actually underpronated a little. I think that is what caused the outside heel rubber to come off on both shoes. The 3.0 has corrected that concern and seems to strike the ground in the center, which makes for a more even wear on the shoe.”.

Besides implementing a lighter upper, the Hoka team redesigned the midsole shape, creating a long channel that runs down the center of the shoe. The rocker also isn’t as exaggerated. What you get is a more stable, smoother ride while racing with propulsion that’s comparable to Hoka’s competitors’. The fit is also broader in the midfoot, making the Cielo X1 3.0 a good choice for runners with wide feet.

Shop Hoka Cielo X1 3 at hoka.com.

Sources indicate that the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 is a prime pick for marathon racing, but it’s also a solid choice for everything else under 26.2 miles. The shoe is so lightweight and delivers such explosive rebound—“you feel like you’re running straight down a trampoline,” states a tester—that it left some of us feeling like we had brownie batter for legs after hard efforts.

According to recent reports, the shoe was the talk of the industry prelaunch after Puma released a study (which the brand sponsored) comparing the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3’s performance to the Nike Alphafly 3, Adidas Adios Pro Evo 1, and Puma Fast-R 2. The study claimed the Elite 3 was 3.15 to 3.62 percent more economical than its competitors.

Putting those numbers aside, our testers agreed this is one powerful racing shoe. “The foam used in this shoe is very noticeable, even when simply starting with a short warmup in the shoe,” notes tester Codi Januszkiewicz, who compares the ride to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4. “Accelerating from a warmup pace straight into some speedwork intervals felt smooth; somehow moving faster in this shoe felt even easier than the warmup.”.

But that power is a lot to handle. “The stability is lacking,” states tester Sean O’Connor. “Almost felt high heelish to me, and it jacked up my calves and feet a little as well. When I ran in them it felt like I was perpetually holding onto the shoe with my feet. I think that's why it made my calves and feet sore.”.

Some can handle the shoe’s intensity over a long period of time. Others may assign the Elite 3 as their mid-distance racing shoe instead. I wore the Elite 3 at a Trackmith 5000 meters over the summer, hitting a PR at 19:12. It’s cush in the heel, but judging by my footfalls, which are heavy, I think racing them in a 26.2 would prolong my usual recovery time postrun.

According to recent reports, when I raced the 2025 London Marathon, I had been training in the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 but instead opted for the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer v2. The Pacer is sleeker and lightweight, unlike the SuperComp Elite v4, which was too beefy for my small frame. The SuperComp Elite v6 is the version of the shoe I would have raced in. Unfortunately, I can’t go back to April 2025. Fortunately for you, the Elite v6 is here just in time for fall marathon season.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe features the brand’s Infinion foam, which was introduced in the 1080v15. The Elite v6’s version of the TPEE- and TPU-based foam is dialed-in for race-ready energy return.

In a recent development, I took the shoe out on a track for a 2 x 2-mile workout at 6:45 pace and the shoes handled turns and helped me hit goal pace. The ride isn’t as aggressive as the Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 or Alphafly, and the cushioning is firmer. Runners with an efficient stride and good form can get away with running marathons and halfs in these shoes, but I’d recommend these for 5Ks and 10Ks because of the firmness and less explosive rebound. The lighter weight makes it ideal for track and medium-distance road races.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 Review.

Though I’ve been racing for 20 years, nothing will get me running an ultra on the trail—which is where our Senior Editor Cat Bowen comes in. Bowen conquered scrambles on steep climbs, dusty ridgelines, gnarly technical trails, and more types of terrain than I run in a year, while testing the long-awaited Tecton X 4.

She gave a shoutout to the hardy Matryx upper that’s “tough as nails” and the grippy 4mm lugs that prevented her from plunging forward. The plus/minus with the shoe is that built-in gaiter collar. Bowen appreciated the extra coverage, but lamented how difficult it was to put on the shoe (we get it: a side zipper would be a good cheat but adds weight). “There is absolutely no reason why this shoe has a front pull tab and nothing in the back,” she wrote in her review.

Still, the new cushioning, Hoka’s ProFly X, and non-winged plate make for a more energized ride that’s less rigid without losing stability. It’s a great shoe for unpredictable. but Bowen urges you to not go the no-sock route.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

Industry observers note that for hours, days, weeks on the trail, there’s the Cloudultra Pro. Bowen has gone through three pairs of the shoe—not because they lack durability but because she likes them so much and runs that much—and appreciates how she doesn’t have to slice the sides. Feet swell during ultras, but it sounds like On prepared for that with its roomy but secure upper.

Another plus in Bowen’s column of ultra shoe musts is the Cloudultra Pro’s lateral stability. Maneuvering over rugged, uneven terrain could spell twisted ankles and slipping and sliding, but the shoe didn’t lead Bowen astray.

Ultrarunner Pat Heine-Holmberg also wore the shoe around Germany’s Zugspitze, where he raced the 102-mile ZUT1000 and ran on “every surface imaginable.”.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com.

It has been revealed that brands are now beginning to release carbon shoes in men’s and women’s sizes. Still, in some cases there’s not much difference between the types of shoes except for maybe the sizing and colors. If the shoes are unisex, it may take a few try-ons to get the fit right. In my unisex racing shoe experience, I’ve found the collar can be loose while the midfoot can be tight. You may want to size up or down, and adopt the heel-lock tying method if the heel area feels too loose.

It has been revealed that do all carbon-fiber plates behave the same way? Sort of. An important lesson to learn here is that the plate isn’t the secret sauce of super shoes—it doesn’t cause propulsion. Instead, the plate, sandwiched between the highly responsive foams, acts as a stabilizer to the super foam. This is why super shoes have such tall stack heights, and why World Athletics caps racing shoe stack height at 40 mm. The super foam—and amount underfoot—is a major advantage.

When choosing a carbon-plate shoe, you’ll want to consider what you’re using it for—racing on the road or trail—and, if possible, have your gait evaluated to determine the best plate angle if you’re looking at shoes specific to running type.

Industry observers note that some plates are full-length or have cutouts. In shoes like the Asics Metaspeed Edge and Metaspeed Sky, the plate’s angle differentiates running types. The Edge’s plate dips lower in the forefoot so cadence runners can roll off their toes faster. The Sky’s plate sits flat in the forefoot, allowing stride runners to leverage bounce on longer steps.

The secret sauce in super shoes is the foam. PEBA (polyether block amide) was once considered the holy grail of all foams and you can still find it in most super shoes, but newer models are using TPEE (thermoplastic polyester elastomer) and A-TPU (aliphatic thermoplastic polyurethane) because they’re more resistant to bottoming out, or going flat. The ride is more durable—and can be quite aggressively bouncy and squishy.

To truly gauge which foam is best for you, trying on the shoe and giving it a run (preferably with some cornering) will help you determine if you want a firmer or squishier ride.

It has been revealed that A carbon-fiber plate shoe is an investment, costing anywhere from $240 upward of $500. There are a couple of things to take into account on a personal level before buying: Can you afford a trainer that’s less durable compared to the standard workhorse shoe, which lasts between 450 to 500 miles?

It has been revealed that while these super shoes are more durable than the ones made eight years ago, they still have a shorter shelf life due to high-performance foams—PEBA and supercritical blends—wearing down faster. Lastly, is the return there? While brands claim these shoes can improve performance, it’s not guaranteed your running economy will improve by around 4 percent.

I spoke with Ted Fitzpatrick, Saucony’s VP of product management, about the differences. He made these key points between carbon and nylon plates:.

Sources indicate that A nylon plate is semirigid with some flexibility. A carbon plate is rigid with little or no flexibility. Popsicle analogy—Imagine the plate as the stick that holds the soft ice cream together. The fundamental use of the plates is to keep the dimensional stability of the foam. With each type of plate, each offers different levels of compliance. The plate maintains the forward rolling effect of super shoes. Carbon is the stiffest, which offers the most concentrated effect of speed roll technology. Nylon still adds stiffness, however, it offers better compliance in how the foot transitions in the gait cycle. Some individuals can respond better to different plates. It is down to what works best for the user.

Recent findings suggest that saucony offers the nylon-plated Endorphin Speed 6, a training shoe that complements its racer, the Endorphin Pro. The shoe can also serve as a more affordable racing shoe, at $180. (The Endorphin Elite 3 and Endorphin Pro 5 cost $290 and $240.).

“The foam is what does the heavy lifting of a super shoe, however it’s the plate that guides how each foam behaves to the user,” claims Fitzpatrick. “It is best to train in both to strengthen and build ‘muscle memory’ into different muscle groups.”.

Industry observers note that however, we wouldn’t recommend solely training in super shoes. For one thing, it would be extremely expensive to use these shoes as daily trainers when they have a shorter shelf life compared to standard everyday shoes. We advise going on a couple of runs before racing in the shoes, to get used to running in them and check for hot spots. While running constantly in these shoes won’t necessarily lead to injury, overuse and the desire to run faster in carbon shoes will likely lead to getting sidelined if you’re not careful.

In a recent development, amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

📅 21 May 2018 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3638 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The 9 Best Stability Shoes for Every Type of Runner

📅 21 May 2018 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Sources indicate that editor’s Note, November 17, 2026: The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is currently our “Best Overall” choice.
  • Some shoes do not have a sexy reputation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that editor’s Note, November 17, 2026: The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is currently our “Best Overall” choice. Recently, the Adrenaline GTS 26 dropped, but we’ve not tested it yet. It’s on the list because we loved the 25 so much. The 25 is currently on sale, so grab it while you can.

Some shoes do not have a sexy reputation. Say “stability shoe” to a certain kind of runner and they’ll look like you just suggested they run their next marathon in Crocs. Stability shoes have a reputation problem, and it’s not entirely undeserved. The stability shoes of the early 2000s were clunky, rigid bricks that treated pronation like a disease to be cured with a slab of hard plastic (looking at you, Saucony Grid Azuras). If you ran through that era, I get why you might have a negative, visceral reaction to the type.

According to recent reports, but here’s the thing: Stability shoes got better. Today’s versions are lighter, softer, and not for anything? Cuter. And they are some of the best shoes you can lace up—not just for overpronators, but for anyone whose form gets sloppy when the miles pile up. I’ve known runners who white-knuckle their way through marathon blocks in neutral racers when a little guidance would have saved their knees, their IT bands, and frankly, their sourpusses. Needing support isn’t taking an L. It’s biomechanics.

Industry observers note that at its simplest, a stability shoe is designed to limit excess inward rolling of the foot (overpronation) after your foot strikes the ground. A little pronation is normal and even beneficial; it helps distribute the shock of the impact. But when your ankle collapses too far inward with every step, that torque travels up the chain to your shins, knees, and hips, and over hundreds of miles it can screw up not just your stride, but your long-term health.

Neutral shoes let your foot do whatever it wants. Stability shoes help guide your foot into a more correct placement, keeping your body more aligned.

From pounding the pavement to scrutinizing performance in our Shoe Lab, the Runner’s World test editors and wear-testers rigorously tested all of our selections. Our process includes exhaustive market research, analysis of user feedback, and consultations with industry experts. This article was written jointly between our editors Amanda Furrer and Cat Bowen. Bowen tends to pronate, especially when she is tired or in a long training block. She has run in all the shoes on this list with the exception of the Nike Structure Plus.

According to recent reports, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is one of the most consistent stability shoes on the market, and the silver anniversary update makes a strong case for why this franchise has lasted 25 years. The substantial news is in the stack: Brooks added 3 mm to the forefoot and 1 mm to the heel, bringing it to 37 mm and 27 mm respectively, and dropped the heel-to-toe offset from 12 mm down to 10 mm for the first time in the shoe’s history.

The new heel bevel is the smoothest the Adrenaline has ever had in the opinion of Bowen, who has put serious miles on this shoe. She also feels as though it’s the most balanced this shoe has ever been, and the most balanced on this list.

“Some stability shoes can be so aggressive that the rails can begin to pinch the lateral sides of the foot during long runs,” she indicates. “The Adrenaline GTS 25 doesn’t do that, and they still have the cushion and push to power your runs.”.

In a recent development, DNA Loft v3 foam carries over from the 24, but the extra volume makes the ride noticeably softer underfoot, especially at heel strike. Guide rails are still doing their thing on the medial and lateral edges—reactive, not prescriptive, engaging only when your stride asks for it. The upper is a breathable engineered mesh that has the benefit of preventing overheating and swamp foot with a stretch knit heel collar that locks down without overcrowding.

Though it should be noted that some testers, including Courtney Kazmierczak, feel as though the collar is a hair too high in the back, which requires some trial and error for sock choice.

Sources indicate that at 10.6 ounces, it’s not light, but it’s not trying to be. This is a daily trainer for runners who want structure and protection. It’s a shoe that simply does not pinch or bite.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a rebuild or huge design change. This is a fine-tuning. The basics are the same; the Adrenaline GTS 26 still uses guide rails as the support system, it has the same stack height, the same drop, the profile hasn’t changed, and the core of the midsole is still the DNA Loft v3 foam.

What did change is that they made it a little bit more breathable by using an engineered mesh upper. The tongue is a bit flatter for a more tuned-in fit, and the heel collar is more refined with a generous pull-tab, which is great for runners with accessibility or limb differences.

The trade-off here is that it is a teensy bit heavier. We’re talking a few tenths of an ounce difference. And, if I’m being the picky and petty editor that I am? I think the colors and design for this model aren’t as cute. I know, I know, lame thing to bring up, but I really just want a stability shoe in a fun neon. Just because I run like a duck doesn’t mean I don’t deserve fun.

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

These may be our best value pick, but they’re also some of the most durable daily stability trainers on this list. “I like the durability and stability of these shoes and the fact that they are lighter than previous models,” said shoe tester Lauren Woodall. “I am able to put more miles on these shoes before they need to be replaced than other running shoes.”.

The thing is, even though it’s heavier, and the durability is noticeable, they’re not bricks. They are your easy run shoes, your throw-on-and-go trainers. They’re not the fastest, but they’re not meant to be. When your body is tired, and you need the assistance of that wave plate and the heft of the Enerzy NXT foam, it’s there for you like an old friend holding out a hand. The guardrails on this shoe aren’t superpowered corrections like they were on earlier models, but the gentle effectiveness of them cannot be overstated. Simply put, these shoes just feel really good on your run.

One note about fit: a few of our testers found that you can get a bit of heel slippage in these. However, Mizuno gives you that extra eyelet for a heel lock, and that can absolutely change the fit of the shoe once you lace up. It’s a point worth remembering.

Shop Men’s at usa.mizuno.com | Shop Women’s at usa.mizuno.com.

The Arahi 9 is Hoka-soft, but not max-cush beefy. It’s a versatile model that does double duty as an everyday trainer or tempo shoe. The brand made small tweaks to the upper for a better fit, and made them a little bit less expensive as well. It’s not a huge redesign as much as it’s a refinement.

You forget the Arahi 9 is a stability shoe because of how streamlined the design looks: it’s sleek and a compliment magnet. Hoka modified the upper to dial in the fit a bit more, make it a little more breathable, and adjust some of the hot points felt in the 8.

Industry observers note that invisible to the eye is the H-Frame system that keeps you stable. The H-Frame is a dense piece of foam in the midsole that’s H-shaped. The result is surprising; you’d think the H-Frame would make the Arahi rigid and heavy, but instead the shoe is lightweight and the ride is smooth. Running in it, Furrer felt like she was gliding.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

There’s something about the Nike Structure Plus that demands attention. In the words of Furrer, “I have a soft spot for this shoe, it’s just so good on long runs.” And that right there is spot on. For the days when you know you have a long run on the calendar, but that long run is full of mixed tempos, hill climbs, potential obstacles, and rough surfaces that you’ll start to feel underfoot after six miles, this is going to be the shoe you reach for. That’s what Nike designed it to handle when it combined the ReactX and ZoomX foams with a dual-zone rubber outsole. It gives you cushion where you need it, flexibility where it matters most, and a nimble feel when you’re dodging pavement cracks.

It has been revealed that arguably the most stylish shoe on this list, Nike really leveled up its stability line with the Structure. It’s also very orthotic-friendly. The collar and the lacing system can handle a lot of pulling, allowing you to get those insoles in correctly. Beyond that, it’s remarkably comfortable as a shoe just to take out and live in. It’s a solid walking shoe, and we love it as a versatile, more cushioned alternative to wear with dressier outfits.

That’s not to say it’s flawless. It’s a bit on the heavier side, and if you’re someone who prefers a shoe that has a lot of responsiveness or bounce, you won’t find it in this shoe. It’s also just a hair on the “runs smaller” side front to back. But other than those small quibbles, it’s a great pair.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

It has been revealed that the differences between the Gel-Kayano 32 and the 33 are important, but not massive. They retooled the design of the support system, employing their FluidSupport tech, which is a bit more malleable than previous iterations, working more with the body’s movements and mechanics. They’ve also softened the foam, updated the fit throughout, and for many runners, it should feel and ride more comfortably.

In a recent development, that being said, it still has all the Asics features you expect and love: a breathable upper, geometry that works to move you forward, and a grippy sole that keeps you upright on wet pavement. It is on the heavier side, but nothing out of the ordinary for a stability shoe, and the collar could have a hair more cushion. However, we love the well-placed heel tab, especially when our hands are sweaty.

Recent findings suggest that the cushion is going to be the biggest win on long-run days. You may not get a ton of energy return, but what you are getting is that added comfort with the guidance that will help you maintain your form and keep you from hating yourself after the run when you’re inevitably lying on the floor propped up on your hands.

Shop Men’s at asics.com |Shop Women’s at asics.com.

In a recent development, the Saucony Guide 19 is a stability shoe that actually earns the word “versatile,” which stability shoes rarely do. Most of them feel like you’re being guided rather than running, but the Guide 19 threads the needle between structured support and genuine responsiveness.

According to recent reports, the foundation is Pwrrun foam, which delivers a cushioned but not marshmallow-soft ride. It’s lively enough to handle tempo work without feeling like you’re fighting the shoe, and cushioned enough that you’re not destroyed after 18 miles. The medial TPU guidance frame offers mild overpronation correction without the brick-like rigidity you get from old-school posts. It’s more a gentle steer rather than having the shoe take the reins and navigate your feet for you.

Sources indicate that for long runs, the 8 mm drop and 32 mm stack height in the heel keep things comfortable for time-on-feet without creating that spongy instability that kills your form late in a run. For daily training, it’s durable and consistent and a shoe you can lace up without thinking too hard about what’s on your schedule.

And it’s just plain comfortable. At least according to our wear-tester Dave Block, who “can’t remember a shoe that’s felt this great.” And even for tempo days on the track, the fit on this shoe just gets it right. It fits snugly enough that at faster paces it doesn’t feel sloppy.It won’t replace a racing flat, but for runners who want one shoe that handles most of their weekly mileage without drama, the Guide 19 makes a strong case.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com |Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

What separates the Hoka Rocket X 3 from other super shoes is its broader base and accommodating fit. The shoe has a winged carbon plate to help with propulsion and a dual-density PEBA midsole to provide high energy return and supportive cushioning. An vital update: a sticky rubber outsole to prevent slipping and sliding when the race forecast predicts rain or snow.

Recent findings suggest that “These shoes were very stable, which is different for a racing shoe,” indicates tester Shane Houghton, an overpronator. “Most super shoes feel kind wobbly but I felt lower to the ground and never felt in danger of rolling an ankle. When I stand in the shoes I feel flat on my feet and I don’t feel any lateral-rocking. I had no anxiety wearing these during loopy intervals or running around curves. The lacing is tight and like the texture of the ribbed laces. It keeps them from coming undone or loosening while running.”.

Sometimes, shoes that are very much stabilizing or stability-adjacent shirk that term for optics. I can’t prove it, but I believe the Nike ACG Zegamas fit that description.

I’ve spent months running in these, and as someone who pronates frequently, I can tell you they deliver the structure and support of a true stability shoe wrapped in the rugged outsole of a trail runner. It comes down to that revised last. The Zegama cups the outer rim of your foot so thoroughly that it holds you locked in place, correcting the roll before it starts.

Industry observers note that the support straps built into the upper wrap all the way around your foot, the padded tongue and lacing lock your midfoot down, and the heel keeps you planted without any slip. It doesn’t feel neutral, but it doesn’t steer you, either. Instead, it almost feels like it’s anticipatory rather than corrective.

Pair that underfoot security with a grippy Vibram outsole and aggressive lugs that bite into mud and wet rock, and you get the best of both worlds—the stable, planted feel of a stability shoe with the traction to handle whatever the trail throws at you.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

With any piece of running equipment, comfort should be your foremost deciding factor. Here are a few thing to consider before your next shoe fitting:.

1) The shoe should have enough room for your toes to splay in the toebox, about a thumbnail’s width from the front of the shoe to the tip of your longest toe.

Sources indicate that 2) The shoe shouldn’t feel too tight or loose around the midfoot area. There are lacing techniques to help modify your shoe’s width, but you should also consider different widths instead of the standard D (men) or B (women) width.

It has been revealed that 3) A secure heel is also paramount, as slippage can cause blisters. The heel-lock lacing method—threading each lace in the etra eyelet next to it to create a loop, then crisscrossing the opposite laces through the loop to create a “lock”—can give you a more secure fit.

It has been revealed that 4) Give the shoes a run at the store or check website’s return/exchange policies. Besides trying on the shoe, the best way to know if it’s comfy is if you run in it, too.

It has been revealed that some runners want maximum cushioning underfoot while others want less padding to experience more ground feel. Fresh foam technology has given us the best of both worlds with plush, high-stacked cushioning that’s lightweight, too. Because of these high stack heights, stability tech is added to help runners run course tangents—and not twist their ankles while doing so.

Industry observers note that still, shoes with thicker cushioning and a high stack (36mm or more) tend to be squishier, making them less stable. Shoes with lower stack heights (32mm or less in the heel) provide a closer-to-the-ground feel and better feedback.

It has been revealed that you don’t have to give up max-cushioning if you’re an overpronator, however. Besides looking for shoes with built-in stability features, like guide rails and stability planes, consider shoes with wide, exaggerated soles, particularly under the heel, and a wider midfoot. Raised sidewalls (the interior padded sides of the shoe) create a snugger fit that will also enhance support, ensuring optimal stability and comfort.

Besides looking for shoes with stability features, you should also consider the type of workouts you’ll be performing in these shoes.

Recent findings suggest that for speedwork, like tempos and track workouts, lightweight trainers (less than 9 ounces for men or 8 ounces for women) with a curved “rocker” midsole help you surge forward. For everyday runs and longer runs, slightly heavier shoes with more padding provide the comfort and durability that you want on a daily training run. Or if you’re interested in venturing off-road, it’s key to have a trail shoe made for rough, undulating terrain.

Do I actually need a stability shoe?

It has been revealed that stability shoes are specifically designed for overpronation, a type of gait pattern when your foot rolls too far inward upon landing. Flat-foot, low arch runners can also benefit from this extra padding in shoes.

Recent findings suggest that not every flat-foot runner or overpronator may need the extra support, however, especially if their feet only have a slight roll. We strongly advise having your gait evaluated by a professional, such as a podiatrist, physical therapist, or movement specialist. They can confirm if you need motion-specific shoes or an orthotic insert.

It has been revealed that the best stability shoes focus on enhancing comfort and promoting a natural gait rather than imposing a harsh, corrective feel. While extra padding may sound like a plus, it can be too prescriptive for some runners. Worst-case scenario: Overcorrecting a neutral stride could increase your chance of injury, rather than make you more comfortable.

If you’re a upcoming runner unsure of your gait pattern, we recommend running in a neutral shoe, like the Hoka Clifton 11s, first.

When should neutral runners consider wearing a stability shoe?

Some shoes with stability tech lend support to late-onset overpronators, i.e., neutral runners whose form becomes erratic midrun due to fatigue. Brands like Brooks and Altra, for instance, use denser foam on the medial and lateral sides of the midsole to help control excessive movement and promote knee and foot alignment, resulting in a more efficient stride.

Is there an adjustment to running in stability shoes?

Industry observers note that as with any running shoe transition, like trying zero-drop trainers for the first time, you’ll want to gradually make the switch if you usually wear neutral shoes. Start with shorter runs and then slowly ramp up mileage or runtime as your body adjusts to the upcoming shoes. Read your body for cues; if you feel some discomfort you may need a slower process before fully committing to stability shoes. Muscle fatigue and pain can also be non-shoe-related and be attributed to overuse. If this is not the issue and it is the shoes, discontinue running in them and talk to a specialist for further evaluation.

Do stability shoes “fix” overpronation?

Recent findings suggest that no. Instead, they support your existing gait pattern. Your shoes can make you feel more comfortable and stable, but it doesn’t change that pattern.

Industry observers note that in the words of Test Editor Morgan Petruny: “Keep in mind that a stability shoe is not a cure-all or magic pill. Rather, it is a tool.”.

In a recent development, overpronation can be due to various factors, including biomechanics, muscle strength, and flexibility, so stability shoes are just one component of a comprehensive approach to managing its negative effects. Strengthening exercises, gait analysis, and proper running form can also play notable roles in that effort.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Just as the seasons change, so do riders’ preferences of which types of riding are preferred. For some, the season for taking the road bike on the local roads starts to fade as temperatures get colder and the gravel trail that parallels the road gets more appealing every degree cooler. It’s time to turn the road bike onto that gravel path.

Industry observers note that many of us have tried to take our road bikes on gravel, and there are steps you can take to get the most out of that underbiked gravel ride. After a recent lunch ride, the question was asked, “how much gravel can you take a road bike on?” Since gravel means different things to different people the easy answer is, it depends, but I wanted to stress test my road bike to find out.

I remember an old-school bike technician I used to work with told me, “you can ride any bike on anything if you are light on the bike and find the right line.” While that may be true, I wanted to find out how I could most comfortably take my road bike on everything that is off-road.

After taking my road bike where it was not designed to go, I learned some limitations as well as some simple part swaps to get the most versatility out of a road bike. Below I’ll touch on those limitations that I found and give you the most impactful changes you can make to your road bike before taking it on gravel. As Doc says to Marty McFly in Back to the Future, “Where we’re going, we don’t need roads.”.

According to recent reports, the bike I decided to do the testing on is my Trek Madone, and I’ve had 700x28mm Pirelli P Zero Race tires pretty much since I’ve built up the bike. Those are by far my favorite road tires for all-around road riding—they’re fast, grip well through turns, and are surprisingly durable for performing so well.

Even though I love those Pirellis for road riding most of the year, I knew I would want to have extra rubber when I’m chattering along through some of the chunkier gravel I’d be testing on. I decided to swap out my tires for a set of the Continental Grand Prix 5000 in 700x32 mm. The maximum tire width on the Gen 8 Trek Madone is 32mm, but these Continental tires only measure just over 30mm because of the internal rim width on the stock Bontrager wheels. I could probably bump up the width a bit more, but I decided to keep the 32mm just in case I knock the wheels out of true during the stress testing.

Going wider with your tires adds an extra bit of compliance and more contact patch—both will help your ride quality when you take your road bike out on gravel. Part of the trick with going wider and bumping down your tire pressure is to make sure your tires are set up as tubeless. Setting your tires up tubeless allows you to run a lower tire pressure without the risk of pinch flats.

Sources indicate that when you take your road bike on gravel, fresh bar tape can help by decreasing a little bit of the vibration. As you ride, most bar tapes compress a bit from the constant pressure of your hands. Some tapes may even start to unravel in sections where you keep your hands a lot—we used to see this a lot when customers couldn’t comfortably reach the hoods. There would be visible wear marks where the rider was keeping their hands on the bars. So replacing your tape at least once a season is a good idea to keep comfort up.

Out of all the bar tape that I’ve tried my favorite for taking a road bike on gravel is the Lizard Skin 3.2 mm Bar Tape. The slightly thicker tape reduces a bit of the chatter in your hands and it’s tacky enough that your hands stay stuck to the bars when you need them to be. This is true on wider tire gravel bikes as well, but it’s especially noticeable when you don’t have the same vibration dampening from a wider tire.

It has been revealed that flat tires happen on any bike, but they can be even more common rolling down a chunky gravel road on your road bike. Correct tire choice, tubeless setups, and riding a bit more cautiously than normal will all help prevent a ride-ending flat tire.

If you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multitool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

If you do get a flat just make sure you are prepared. At a minimum I typically carry at least one tube, tire levers, at least one type of inflation, and a good multi tool. If I’m going to be far from my car, home, or if I’ll be out of cell phone service I’ll bring more than one tube—especially on an underbiking ride. I’ve been stuck out on a ride after burning through my lone spare tube, so now I like having two on rides like this. A few pieces of extra additions to your flat kit are: zip ties, a tire boot or dollar bill, and a tubeless plug kit if you’re running tubeless tires.

It has been revealed that keep in mind it’s still possible to get flat tires with tubeless tires. A few years ago I took my road bike out on a local gravel ride and I bumped my tire pressure down to have a little more comfort and traction on my skinny road tires. I was rolling through some gravel and I hit a rock with my rear wheel hard enough for the tire to get pinched against the rim and put a good slice in my tire. Luckily I brought a tire boot (I used a dollar bill) and an extra tube so I was able to pedal back to the shop. In a pinch I’ve used things like candy wrappers or leaves as a very temporary tire boot. They don’t take up much room in your pack, so if you bring one in your pack there is no need to MacGyver anything on the side of the trail.

If you only have a road bike and want to occasionally ride gravel I would strongly consider getting a second wheelset to ride gravel. If you have one wheel set for gravel and one for pavement you can easily swap wheel sets when you want to ride one discipline versus the other. Set up the wheels with a cassette with the same gear range, same size rotors, and the widest tires your frame and fork can fit—suddenly you have two bikes in one.

As I was taking my road bike on exceedingly questionable terrain I thought, what would most people actually be okay with riding this bike on? As I rolled my Madone into some singletrack it was promptly apparent most people wouldn’t be stoked to follow behind me. Insufficient tire clearance, room for tread, and lack of suspension might be the first reasons you’d think of why a road bike isn’t going to perform well on singletrack (and you’re absolutely right). The geometry of the Madone didn’t give the handling needed to reasonably navigate through the tight trails in the woods.

According to recent reports, the next category is where we start to delve into true gravel: doubletrack, jeep roads, and limited maintenance gravel. This is where I started to see the road bike actually perform reasonably well. The extra tire width combined with bumping down the tire pressure allowed the bike to feel reasonably compliant rolling through the varying surfaces. However, I really felt the times I caught a small rock that was hiding underneath the leaves.

In a recent development, riding local gravel roads and canal trails may have been bumpy, but it was most certainly doable. I noticed I was bumping around a lot, and I felt like I was putting in more effort to match my typical effort on the same segments I usually ride with a gravel bike. Especially when I started to ride through gravel after a bit of rain or sections that were covered in wet leaves I wished for a wider tire with more tread. I had to keep some of the descents a little more tame compared to normal, but on my local gravel climbs I was rolling up faster and more efficiently than normal. That is, until my rear tire would lose traction and I would burn all my matches trying to keep the bike both upright and going up.

Industry observers note that even with that being the case, so many modern road bikes now offer tire clearance to get a cyclocross tire set up. If I were committing to my road bike as a gravel-to-road crossover bike for the winter I would set it up with some fast-rolling tubeless cyclocross tires, put on latest bar tape, put an extra tube in my flat pack, and let it ride.
